}}The '''Green Party of Aotearoa New Zealand''' ({{langx|mi|Rōpū Kākāriki o Aotearoa, Niu Tireni}}),<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.greens.org.nz/charter|title=Our Charter|publisher=Green Party of Aotearoa New Zealand|access-date=7 April 2023}}</ref> commonly known as '''the Greens''' or the '''Green Party''',<ref name="Miller">{{cite book|last1=Miller|first1=Raymond|title=Democracy in New Zealand|date=2015|publisher=Auckland University Press|page=169|isbn=9781775588085|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=1T93CQAAQBAJ&pg=PT146}}</ref><ref name="Mazzoleni">{{cite book|last1=Mazzoleni|first1=Juliet Roper; Christina Holtz-Bacha; Gianpietro|title=The Politics of Representation: Election Campaigning and Proportional Representation|date=2004|publisher=Lang|location=New York, NY [u.a.]|isbn=9780820461489|page=40}}</ref> are a [[Environmentalism|environmentalist]] and [[Social democracy|social democratic]] [[Green party|Green political party]] in New Zealand. They are currently the third largest party in the [[New Zealand House of Representatives|House of Representatives]], with 15 of the 120 members, sitting as the second largest opposition party.<ref name="results2023">{{cite web |date=14 October 2023 |title=2023 General Election – Official Result |url=https://elections.nz/media-and-news/2023/official-results-for-the-2023-general-election/ |access-date=14 October 2023 |website=Electoral Commission}}</ref>

The party has helped form government three times, providing confidence and supply to the [[Fifth Labour Government of New Zealand|Labour–Alliance coalition]] from 1999 to 2002, the [[First term of the Sixth Labour Government of New Zealand|Labour–New Zealand First coalition]] from 2017 to 2020, and the [[Second term of the Sixth Labour Government of New Zealand|Labour majority government]] from 2020 to 2023. During the latter two of these, the party had ministers outside [[Cabinet of New Zealand|cabinet]].

The party traces its origins to the [[Values Party]] that was founded in 1972. In 1990, the current party was created and was a part of the [[Alliance (New Zealand political party)|Alliance]] from 1991 until 1997. The party first won seats in Parliament in 1996 as part of the Alliance. Since 1997, it has contested general elections independently of the now mainly defunct Alliance, and has achieved above the 5% threshold each time. The party's weakest showing was 2005 when it elected 6 members on 5.3% of the party vote; its strongest was 2023 when it elected 15 members on 11.6% of the party vote (including three electorate MPs).

The party has also successfully ran candidates in local body elections; some candidates run under the Green Party brand whilst others run as independents with endorsement. Following the [[2025 New Zealand local elections|2025 local elections]], the party has thirteen regional and local councillors, and one elected mayor. In Auckland, some Green members run as [[City Vision]] candidates, particularly in the city centre. In Christchurch, Green members typically run as part of [[The People's Choice (political ticket)|The People's Choice]]. Green endorsed mayors have been elected in Dunedin, Wellington, and Whakatāne.

== Precursors ==
{{See also|Environmental movement in New Zealand}}
The Green Party traces its origins to the [[Values Party]],<ref name="Green History">{{cite web |url=http://greens.org.nz/about/history.htm |title=Greens in Time and Space: The History of The Green Party 1972–1999 |author=Christine Dann |publisher=Green Party of Aotearoa New Zealand |access-date=29 June 2008 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20081010175959/http://www.greens.org.nz/about/history.htm |archive-date=10 October 2008 }}
</ref> the world's first national-level environmentalist party.<ref>{{cite web|title=History |url=https://www.greenparty.ca/en/party/history|website=Green Party of Canada|quote=The first national green party in the world, the Values Party, was started in the early 1970s in New Zealand.}}</ref><ref>{{cite book|last1=Barry|first1=John|last2=Frankland|first2=E. Gene|title=International Encyclopedia of Environmental Politics|date=2014|publisher=Routledge|isbn=9781135553968|page=461|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=BXzsAgAAQBAJ&pg=PA461|language=en}}</ref> The Values Party originated in 1972 at [[Victoria University of Wellington]].<ref name="Green History" /><ref>{{cite news|last=O'Brien|first=Tova|title=Forty years since first green party|url=http://www.newshub.co.nz/politics/forty-years-since-first-green-party-2012060121|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161220073801/http://www.newshub.co.nz/politics/forty-years-since-first-green-party-2012060121|url-status=dead|archive-date=20 December 2016|newspaper=[[Newshub]]|access-date=5 February 2017|date=1 June 2012}}</ref> 

While it gained a measure of public support in several elections, the [[First-past-the-post voting|first-past-the-post]] electoral system meant that the party did not win any seats in Parliament. Some of the founding members of the Green Party, including [[Jeanette Fitzsimons]], [[Rod Donald]] and [[Mike Ward (New Zealand politician)|Mike Ward]], had been active members of the Values Party at the outset of the [[Green movement]] in the 1970s.{{Citation needed|date=October 2026}}

In 1989, multiple candidates stood for local government positions under a "green" label. It saw the election of New Zealand's first "green" city councillor, [[Stephen Rainbow]], in Wellington.<ref>{{Cite news |first=Shani |last=Naylor |title=Green's a good colour for Steve Rainbow |work=[[The Evening Post (New Zealand)|The Evening Post]] |date=8 January 1990 |page= }}</ref> He was joined the next year by councillor Merrin Downing, who left the [[Wellington Citizens' Association|Citizens' Association]] to join the Greens.<ref>{{Cite news |title=Cr Downing drops Citizens for Greens |work=[[The Evening Post (New Zealand)|The Evening Post]] |date=5 October 1990 |page= }}</ref>

In May 1990, remnants of the Values Party merged with a number of other environmentalist organisations to form the modern Green Party.<ref>{{Cite news |title=Greens merge |work=[[Auckland Star]] |date=28 May 1990 |page=A3 }}</ref> This sparked a resurgence of support, with the new group winning 6.85% of the vote (but no seats) in the [[1990 New Zealand general election|1990 election]].
==History==
===The Alliance (1991–1997)===
[[File:Jeanette Fitzsimons.jpg|thumb|upright|Former Green Party co-leader [[Jeanette Fitzsimons]]]]The newly formed Green Party became a founding member of the [[Alliance (New Zealand political party)|Alliance]], a five-party grouping that also included the [[New Zealand Democratic Party for Social Credit|Democrats]], [[New Zealand Liberal Party (1991)|Liberals]], [[Mana Motuhake (political party)|Mana Motuhake]] and [[NewLabour Party (New Zealand)|NewLabour Party]].<ref>{{cite news |title=Alliance born with eye on Tamaki win |author=Orsman, Bernard |work=[[The New Zealand Herald]] |date=2 December 1991 |page=1 }}</ref> Immediately prior to this there had been limited co-operation between the parties running joint candidates in several local by-elections in Auckland. One candidate, Ruth Norman, was from the Greens and was elected to the [[Auckland Regional Council]].<ref>{{cite news |title=Voters go for new parties |work=[[The New Zealand Herald]] |date=28 November 1991 |page=1 }}</ref> At the Alliance's inaugural party conference in November 1992, party members elected [[Jeanette Fitzsimons]] as one of the co-deputy leaders of the Alliance.<ref>{{cite news |title=Alliance gets three-way leadership |author=Laugesen, Ruth |work=[[The Dominion (Wellington)|The Dominion]] |date=16 November 1992 |page=2 }}</ref>

The party contested the [[1993 New Zealand general election|1993]] and [[1996 New Zealand general election|1996 election]]s as part of the Alliance.<ref name="Green History" /> Membership in the Alliance was a controversial decision with a sizeable minority in the party remaining opposed to it. Consequently, the party was plagued in the following few years by persistent calls for departure from the Alliance.<ref>{{cite news |title=No plans for Greens to leave |newspaper=[[The New Zealand Herald]] |date=11 November 1993 |page=5 }}</ref> Over time the issue became a more divisive issue internally until eventually a splinter party, the [[Progressive Green Party (New Zealand)|Progressive Green Party]], was set up by members who were unhappy at the direction of the Alliance, which they believed was too left-wing and too focused on social justice issues, detracting focus from environmental issues.<ref>{{cite news |author=Scherer, Karyn |title=Dissident Greens may form new party |newspaper=[[The Evening Post (New Zealand)|The Evening Post]] |date=3 May 1994 }}</ref><ref>{{cite news |author=Edwards, Brent |title=Breakaway party no threat, says Alliance leader |newspaper=[[The Evening Post (New Zealand)|The Evening Post]] |date=16 May 1994 }}</ref>

Until the 1995 annual conference in [[Taupō]], the party had no elected leaders. At that conference, Jeanette Fitzsimons was elected unopposed as female co-leader, and Rod Donald defeated Joel Cayford and Mike Smith in a three-way contest to become male co-leader.<ref>{{cite news|work=[[The Evening Post (Wellington)|The Evening Post]] |page=2 |title=Greens seek higher profile |date=22 May 1995 }}</ref>

After New Zealand adopted the [[Mixed-member proportional representation|mixed-member proportional]] (MMP) electoral system in 1996, the Alliance gained entry to Parliament, bringing three Green [[list MP]]s with them: Jeanette Fitzsimons, Rod Donald and [[Phillida Bunkle]].<ref>{{cite news |last=White |first=Mike |title=Are the Greens still scary? A political power comes of age |url=https://www.noted.co.nz/currently/currently-politics/are-the-greens-still-scary-a-political-power-comes-of-age |access-date=10 August 2020 |work=[[North & South (New Zealand magazine)|North & South]] |date=30 May 2017 |language=en-NZ |archive-date=21 April 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200421124344/https://www.noted.co.nz/currently/currently-politics/are-the-greens-still-scary-a-political-power-comes-of-age |url-status=dead }}</ref>

In 1997, feeling that membership of the Alliance had subsumed their identity, the party made the decision to stand candidates independently of the Alliance at the next election.<ref name="Green History" /> While most Green party members left the Alliance, some decided to leave the Green Party and stay in the Alliance (including Bunkle, who would later be appointed [[Minister of Customs (New Zealand)|Minister of Customs]] in the [[Fifth Labour Government of New Zealand|Labour-Alliance coalition government]]). Conversely, some of the Alliance party members, who joined the Alliance via other parties, decided to leave the Alliance and join the Green Party. These notably included [[Sue Bradford]] and [[Keith Locke]], who both joined the Alliance from NewLabour.<ref name="Vowels et al">{{cite book |last1=Vowels|first1=Jack|last2=Coffé |first2=Hilde |last3=Curtin |first3=Jennifer |chapter=The 2014 New Zealand election in perspective |title=A Bark but No Bite |date=2017 |pages=1–24 |publisher=ANU Press|jstor=j.ctt1vw0p68.7|isbn=9781760461355}}</ref>

===Green Party in Parliament===
[[File:RodDonaldGreenMP.jpg|upright|thumb|Former Green Party co-leader [[Rod Donald]].]]

====1999 election====
In the [[1999 New Zealand general election|1999 election]], the Greens gained 5.16% of the [[party vote]] and seven seats in Parliament. Fitzsimons also won the electorate seat of [[Coromandel (New Zealand electorate)|Coromandel]]; it is believed that this is the first time a Green candidate won a first-past-the-post parliamentary election.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://home.greens.org.nz/history-green-party#toc-the-1990s-and-the-first-green-party-campaign|title=The History of The Green Party|publisher=Green Party of Aotearoa New Zealand|access-date=28 August 2015|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180128024547/https://home.greens.org.nz/history-green-party#toc-the-1990s-and-the-first-green-party-campaign|archive-date=28 January 2018|url-status=dead}}</ref> During the ten days it took to count special votes and confirm Fitzsimons' election, [[New Zealand Labour Party|Labour]] concluded a coalition agreement with the Alliance which excluded the Greens. However, the party supported the government on [[confidence and supply]] in return for some input into the budget and legislation. This led to the Greens gaining a $15&nbsp;million energy efficiency and environmental package in the new government's first budget.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://greens.org.nz/docs/press/000615budget01-leaders.htm |title=Green Budget Package far reaching |publisher=Green Party of Aotearoa New Zealand |date=15 June 2000 |access-date=29 June 2008 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120217220028/http://www.greens.org.nz/docs/press/000615budget01-leaders.htm |archive-date=17 February 2012 |url-status=dead }}</ref> Over the term, the Greens developed a good working relationship with the government and also had some input into policy, notably Sue Bradford's amendments to the [[Employment Relations Act 2000]].{{Citation needed|date=July 2008}}

====2002 election====
In the [[2002 New Zealand general election|2002 election]], the Greens polled 7.00%, increasing their strength in Parliament to nine seats, although they lost the Coromandel electorate.<ref name="2002 election">{{cite web |title=Official Count Results – Overall Status |url= http://www.electionresults.govt.nz/electionresults_2002/partystatus.html |publisher=Electoral Commission |access-date=7 August 2013}}</ref><ref name="Coromandel, 2002">{{cite web |title=Official Count Results – Coromandel |url= http://www.electionresults.govt.nz/electionresults_2002/electorate-9.html |publisher=Electoral Commission |access-date=7 August 2013}}</ref> The electoral campaign featured strong tensions between the Greens and Labour. The Greens sharply criticised Labour for its plans to allow a moratorium on genetic engineering to expire, and believing that Labour would require their support to form a government, intended to make the extension of this moratorium a non-negotiable part of any deal.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Boston |first1=Jonathan |last2=Church |first2=Stephen |last3=Levine |first3=Stephen |title=New Zealand Votes: The General Election of 2002 |year=2003 |publisher=Victoria University Press |isbn=978-0-86473-468-6 |page=275 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=N-ql-Xs9hhkC |language=en}}</ref> After the election, however, Labour and their coalition partner, the Jim Anderton-led [[New Zealand Progressive Party|Progressive Coalition]], instead opted to rely on support from [[United Future New Zealand|United Future]], at that time a party with conservative Christian overtones.

Although the Greens no longer had any input into the budget, they maintained a close working relationship with the government, and the Greens remained involved in the legislation process. Often the government needed to rely on Green votes in the [[New Zealand House of Representatives|House]] to pass progressive legislation not approved by United Future.{{citation needed|date=February 2024}} The government won praise from political commentators for juggling the two diametrically-opposed parties.

====2005 election====
In the [[2005 New Zealand general election|2005 election]], the Greens won 5.30%, returning six of their MPs to Parliament. Despite expressing clear support for a [[New Zealand Labour Party|Labour]]-led government during the campaign,<ref>{{cite web |url= http://home.nzcity.co.nz/news/article.aspx?id=54847&cat=975 |title=Greens talk about coalition options |publisher=NZCity |date=12 September 2005 |access-date=28 June 2008}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.nzherald.co.nz/section/1/story.cfm?c_id=1&objectid=10339337 |title=Interview: Jeanette Fitzsimons, Green Party co-leader |work=[[The New Zealand Herald]] |date=6 August 2005 |access-date=28 June 2008}}</ref> they were excluded from the resulting coalition, due to a refusal by United Future and NZ First to work with the Greens in cabinet.<ref name="NZ_Herald_10346236">{{cite news|author=Thomson, Ainsley|date=19 September 2005|title=United's 'Mr Reasonable' makes withering attack on Green Party|work=[[The New Zealand Herald]]|url=http://www.nzherald.co.nz/election-2005/news/article.cfm?c_id=1500891&objectid=10346236|access-date=30 October 2011}}</ref> They were, however, able to negotiate a cooperation agreement which saw limited input into the budget and broad consultation on policy.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.beehive.govt.nz/sites/all/files/Green.pdf |title=Labour led Government Co-operation Agreement with the Green Party |date=17 October 2005 |access-date=28 June 2008 |archive-date=22 April 2014 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140422192243/http://www.beehive.govt.nz/sites/all/files/Green.pdf |url-status=dead }}</ref> Both co-leaders were appointed as government spokespeople outside cabinet, with Fitzsimons responsible for Energy Efficiency, and Donald responsible for the [[Buy Kiwi Made]] campaign. However, Rod Donald died the day before Parliament was due to sit and the position of government spokesperson on Buy Kiwi Made was filled by [[Sue Bradford]].<ref>{{cite web |url= http://www.nzherald.co.nz/section/1/story.cfm?c_id=1&ObjectID=10353831 |title=Greens co-leader dies |work=[[The New Zealand Herald]] |date=6 November 2006 |access-date=28 June 2008}}</ref> [[Nándor Tánczos]] took up the vacant list position<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.elections.org.nz/news/ceo-media-green-141105.html |title=New list MP for Green Party |publisher=New Zealand Electoral Commission |date=14 November 2005 |access-date=28 June 2008 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20061002114722/http://www.elections.org.nz/news/ceo-media-green-141105.html |archive-date=2 October 2006 |url-status=dead }}</ref> and the co-leader position remained vacant until a new co-leader, [[Russel Norman]] was elected at their 2006 [[annual general meeting]]. The other contenders for the position were Nándor Tánczos, [[David Clendon]] and former MP [[Mike Ward (New Zealand politician)|Mike Ward]].<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.greens.org.nz/searchdocs/PR9864.html |title=Green Co-Leader announced |publisher=Green Party of Aotearoa New Zealand |date=3 June 2006 |access-date=28 June 2008 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20081123060613/http://greens.org.nz/searchdocs/PR9864.html |archive-date=23 November 2008 }}</ref>
Bradford also introduced, in 2005, the [[Private member's bill|members' bill]] that would become the [[Crimes (Substituted Section 59) Amendment Act 2007]]. The bill sought to outlaw the legal defence of "reasonable force" for parents prosecuted for assault against children. It led to widespread debate and accusations that MPs supporting the bill were fostering a '[[nanny state]]' approach. Despite this, the Bill became law after it passed its third reading on 16 May 2007 with an overwhelming majority of 113 votes for and 7 votes against.<ref>{{cite news | title = Anti-smacking bill becomes law | publisher = NZPA | date = 16 May 2007 | url = http://www.nzherald.co.nz/section/1/story.cfm?c_id=1&objectid=10440080 | access-date = 16 May 2007}}</ref>

====2008 election====
In the [[2008 New Zealand general election|2008 election]], the Greens increased their share of the vote to 6.72%, enough for 9 MPs, even though there was a swing throughout the country to the [[New Zealand National Party|National Party]]. This initially gave the Greens two extra MPs, but counting the special votes brought in a third.<ref name="NZHerald_10544503">{{cite web|url=http://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/news/article.cfm?c_id=1&objectid=10544503|title=Special votes see Greens gain seat, Nats lose|date=22 November 2008|work=[[The New Zealand Herald]]|access-date=22 November 2008}}</ref> They became the third largest parliamentary party in New Zealand, and signed a [[memorandum of understanding]] with the governing [[New Zealand National Party|National Party]].

[[Metiria Turei]] was elected at the 2009 annual general meeting after former female co-leader [[Jeanette Fitzsimons]] stood down as an MP in February 2009.<ref>{{cite web |title=Fitzsimons to Pass Co-leadership Torch in June |url=https://home.greens.org.nz/press-releases/fitzsimons-pass-co-leadership-torch-june |publisher=Green Party of Aotearoa New Zealand |access-date=4 October 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171004085421/https://home.greens.org.nz/press-releases/fitzsimons-pass-co-leadership-torch-june |archive-date=4 October 2017 |url-status=dead }}</ref><ref>{{cite web|title=Turei picked as new Greens co-leader|url=http://tvnz.co.nz/politics-news/turei-picked-new-greens-co-leader-2763231|publisher=[[TVNZ]] |work=[[Newstalk ZB]]/[[1News]]|access-date=5 October 2012|year=2009|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090531072801/http://tvnz.co.nz/politics-news/turei-picked-new-greens-co-leader-2763231|archive-date=31 May 2009|language=en-NZ}}</ref>

====2011 election====
In the [[2011 New Zealand general election|2011 election]], the Green Party received nearly a quarter of a million party votes (247,372), equating to 11.06% of the total valid party votes nationwide, earning them 14 seats in the 50th Parliament. Preliminary results on election night showed them with 10.6% of the vote, equivalent to 13 seats, but special votes increased their support enough to gain an extra seat.<ref>{{cite news|title=First deaf MP to join Parliament|url=http://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/news/article.cfm?c_id=1&objectid=10772275|access-date=10 December 2011|work= [[The New Zealand Herald]]|date=10 December 2011}}</ref> They remained the third largest parliamentary party in New Zealand.<ref name="STUFF">{{cite web|url=http://www.stuff.co.nz/national/politics/election-results/official-count |title=Official Count|date=26 November 2011|publisher=[[Stuff (website)|Stuff]] |access-date=26 November 2011}}</ref>

====2014 election====
In the [[2014 New Zealand general election|2014 general election]], the Green Party's share of the party vote fell slightly to 10.70%. Despite this, they retained all of their 14 seats and remained the third largest party in Parliament.<ref name="Vowels et al" />

James Shaw was elected at the party's 2015 annual general meeting over fellow MPs [[Gareth Hughes (politician)|Gareth Hughes]] and [[Kevin Hague]], and party member [[Vernon Tava]]. He succeeded [[Russel Norman]], who resigned in November 2015 to work as Executive Director of [[Greenpeace Aotearoa New Zealand]].<ref>{{cite news | url=http://www.radionz.co.nz/news/political/288456/goodbye-greens,-hello-greenpeace | title=Russel Norman quits Greens for Greenpeace | work=[[Radio New Zealand]] | date=31 October 2015 | access-date=7 November 2015 | author=Edwards, Brent}}</ref>

====2017 election====
In their [[2017 New Zealand general election|2017 election]] campaign launch on 9 July 2017, the Green Party proposed charging bottling companies a 10% tax for exporting water, with the revenue being split between local councils and Māori tribes or iwi. They also announced that they would ban new resource consents for bottling companies until the establishment of a new comprehensive commercial water pricing scheme.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Heron|first1=Mei |title=Green Party proposes tighter rules for water sales|url=http://www.radionz.co.nz/news/political/334762/green-party-proposes-tighter-rules-for-water-sales|access-date=12 October 2017|publisher=[[Radio New Zealand]] |date=9 July 2017}}</ref>

In July 2017, co-leader Metiria Turei criticised the populist [[New Zealand First]] party and its leader [[Winston Peters]] for alleged racism, particularly [[anti-immigration|towards immigration]].<ref name="Turei vs Peters">{{cite news|last1=Trevett|first1=Claire|title=Green Party's Metiria Turei 'racist' call riles NZ First's Winston Peters|url=http://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/news/article.cfm?c_id=1&objectid=11888053|access-date=11 October 2017|work= [[The New Zealand Herald]]|date=9 July 2017}}</ref> List MP [[Barry Coates]] penned an article in the left-wing "The Daily Blog" claiming that the Greens would call a snap election rather than be excluded from a prospective Labour and New Zealand First coalition government.<ref>{{cite web|last1=Coates|first1=Barry|title=Great Together|url=https://thedailyblog.co.nz/2017/07/11/great-together/|website=The Daily Blog|date=11 July 2017 |access-date=11 October 2017}}</ref> Turei and Coates' comments were fiercely criticised by both Peters and New Zealand First MP [[Tracey Martin]], who warned that this would affect post-election negotiations between the two parties. Fellow co-leader Shaw later clarified that Coates' remarks did not represent Green Party policy.<ref>{{cite news|title=Green MP's comments on NZ First the 'height of stupidity' – Winston Peters|url=http://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/news/article.cfm?c_id=1&objectid=11889937|access-date=11 October 2017|work= [[The New Zealand Herald]]|date=13 July 2017}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|last1=Lynch|first1=Jenna|title=Green MP threatens new election if Labour goes with NZ First|url=http://www.newshub.co.nz/home/politics/2017/07/green-mp-threatens-new-election-if-labour-goes-with-nz-first.html|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170712211544/http://www.newshub.co.nz/home/politics/2017/07/green-mp-threatens-new-election-if-labour-goes-with-nz-first.html|url-status=dead|archive-date=12 July 2017|access-date=11 October 2017|publisher=[[Newshub]]|date=13 July 2017}}</ref>

On 16 July, in order to raise awareness of the inadequacies of the welfare system, Turei disclosed that she had committed benefit fraud in the past.<ref name="Metiria Turei’s speech to the Green Party 2017 AGM">{{cite web |last1=Green Party |title=Mending the Safety Net – Metiria Turei's speech to the Green Party 2017 AGM |url=http://www.scoop.co.nz/stories/PA1707/S00237/speech-turei-mending-the-safety-net.htm |website=Scoop |publisher=Scoop Media |access-date=1 September 2018}}</ref> Turei also advocated for raising the domestic purposes benefit for families during the Green Party's electoral campaign. Her disclosure generated considerable interest from the media, politicians, and the New Zealand blogosphere.<ref>{{cite news|last1=Kirk|first1=Stacey|title=Benefit raise, tax cuts for poorest and hikes for wealthy in new Greens policy|url=https://www.stuff.co.nz/national/politics/94777073/benefit-raise-tax-cuts-for-poorest-and-hikes-for-wealthy-in-news-greens-policy|access-date=26 July 2017|agency=[[Stuff (website)|Stuff]] |date=16 July 2017}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|title='We can never condone breaking the rules' – Andrew Little won't support Metiria Turei's stance of not condemning benefit fraudsters|url=https://www.tvnz.co.nz/one-news/new-zealand/we-can-never-condone-breaking-rules-andrew-little-wont-support-metiria-tureis-stance-not-condemning-benefit-fraudsters|access-date=26 July 2017|publisher=[[1News]]|date=26 July 2017}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|last1=Soper|first1=Barry|title=Metiria Turei vs Barry Soper: Listen to heated debate|url=http://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/news/article.cfm?c_id=1&objectid=11895020|access-date=26 July 2017|work=[[The New Zealand Herald]]|date=25 July 2017}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|last1=Gower|first1=Patrick|title=Patrick Gower: Metiria Turei's political fraud is ripping off the New Zealand public|url=http://www.newshub.co.nz/home/election/2017/07/patrick-gower-metiria-turei-s-political-fraud-is-ripping-off-the-new-zealand-public.html|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170726022646/http://www.newshub.co.nz/home/election/2017/07/patrick-gower-metiria-turei-s-political-fraud-is-ripping-off-the-new-zealand-public.html|url-status=dead|archive-date=26 July 2017|access-date=26 July 2017|publisher=[[Newshub]]|date=26 July 2017}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|last1=Trotter|first1=Chris|title=Sins Of Admission – critiquing John Armstrong's attack on Metiria|url=https://thedailyblog.co.nz/2017/07/22/sins-of-admission-critiquing-john-armstrongs-attack-on-metiria/|website=The Daily Blog|date=22 July 2017 |access-date=26 July 2017}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|last1=Bradbury|first1=Martyn|title=The importance of what Metiria has done and why we should all support her|url=https://thedailyblog.co.nz/2017/07/26/the-importance-of-what-metiria-has-done-and-why-we-should-all-support-her/|website=The Daily Blog|date=26 July 2017 |access-date=26 July 2017}}</ref> Initially the increased coverage lead to the Greens having their highest poll result ever of 15% while Labour had its lowest in 20 years at 24%, eventually leading to Andrew Little's resignation.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Aotearoa |first=RNZ {{!}} Te Reo Irirangi o |date=1 August 2017 |title=Little walks the plank |url=https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/politics/336219/little-walks-the-plank |access-date=11 October 2026 |website=RNZ |language=en-nz}}</ref> However media coverage eventual went against Turei. On 7 August, Green MPs [[Kennedy Graham]] and party whip [[David Clendon]] resigned as Green Party candidates due to their disagreement with Turei's actions and handling of the situation. They formally resigned from the Green Party's parliamentary caucus the following day after the party made moves to remove them "involuntarily."<ref name="clendon-graham-resign">{{cite web|url=https://www.stuff.co.nz/national/politics/95549623/greens-in-crisis-metiria-turei-stays-on-despite-mps-quitting|title=Rogue Green MPs withdraw from caucus – party 'united' behind co-leader Metiria Turei|access-date=8 August 2017|date=8 August 2017|publisher=Stuff.co.nz }}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.scoop.co.nz/stories/PA1708/S00157/joint-statement-david-clendon-and-kennedy-graham.htm|title=Joint Statement David Clendon and Kennedy Graham|date=8 August 2017|access-date=13 August 2017|publisher=Green Party of Aotearoa New Zealand|via=[[Scoop (website)|Scoop.co.nz]]}}</ref>
 
On 9 August, Turei resigned as co-leader and as a list candidate, stating that the media scrutiny on her family had become unbearable. James Shaw remained the Green Party's sole leader for the 2017 election.<ref>{{Cite news|url=http://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/news/article.cfm?c_id=1&objectid=11901089|title=Green Party co-leader Metiria Turei resigns|last=Davison|first=Isaac|date=9 August 2017|work=[[The New Zealand Herald]]|access-date=9 August 2017}}</ref><ref name="rnz-turei-resigns">{{cite web|url=http://www.radionz.co.nz/news/political/336833/green-party-co-leader-metiria-turei-resigns|title=Green Party co-leader Metiria Turei resigns|access-date=12 August 2017|date=9 August 2017|publisher=[[Radio New Zealand]]}}</ref> Clendon stated that he would not be returning to the Green Party list despite Turei's resignation. Graham sought to return to the party list, but this was declined on 12 August by the Green Party Executive. Leader James Shaw indicated that there was considerable animosity within the party towards Clendon and Graham for their actions.<ref>{{cite news|title=David Clendon not planning return to Green Party list|url=https://www.tvnz.co.nz/one-news/new-zealand/david-clendon-not-planning-return-green-party-list|access-date=12 August 2017|agency=TVNZ|date=10 August 2017}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|title=Kennedy Graham denied Green candidacy|url=http://www.radionz.co.nz/news/political/337030/kennedy-graham-denied-greens-candidacy|access-date=12 August 2017|publisher=[[Radio New Zealand]]|date=12 August 2017}}</ref>

On 17 August, it was reported that the Green Party had fallen by 11 points to 4% in the ''[[1News]]''–Colmar Brunton Poll, below the 5% [[Electoral threshold|threshold]] needed to enter Parliament under [[Electoral system of New Zealand#MMP in New Zealand|New Zealand's mixed-member proportional system]]. The party's sharp drop in the opinion poll was attributed to negative publicity around the Green Party's infighting and the ascension of [[Jacinda Ardern]] as leader of the centre-left [[Labour Party of New Zealand|Labour Party]], the Greens' nominal ally.<ref>{{cite news|last1=Small|first1=Vernon|title=Green Party out of Parliament, Labour surges in new poll|url=https://www.stuff.co.nz/national/politics/95896855/green-party-out-of-parliament-labour-surges-in-new-poll|access-date=19 August 2017|agency=[[Stuff (website)|Stuff]]|date=17 August 2017}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|title=Greens could be out of Parliament, poll reveals|url=http://www.newshub.co.nz/home/election/2017/08/greens-could-be-out-of-parliament-poll-reveals.html|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170819061621/http://www.newshub.co.nz/home/election/2017/08/greens-could-be-out-of-parliament-poll-reveals.html|url-status=dead|archive-date=19 August 2017|access-date=19 August 2017|agency=[[Newshub]]|date=17 August 2017}}</ref> By contrast, the Roy Morgan opinion poll placed public support for the Green Party at 9%.<ref>{{cite news|last1=Keall|first1=Chris|title=Roy Morgan poll better news for Greens|url=https://www.nbr.co.nz/article/roy-morgan-poll-better-news-greens-ck-206672|access-date=19 August 2017|work=[[National Business Review]]|date=19 August 2017}}</ref>

The 2017 general election returned eight list MPs, with 6.3% of the party vote.<ref name="2017 general election results">{{cite web|title=2017 General Election – Official Result|url=http://www.electionresults.govt.nz/electionresults_2017/|access-date=7 October 2017|publisher=[[Electoral Commission (New Zealand)|New Zealand Electoral Commission]]}}</ref> The Green parliamentary caucus' newest members were [[Chlöe Swarbrick]], who became the [[Baby of the House#New Zealand|youngest member]] of the House, and [[Golriz Ghahraman]], the first [[refugee]] member of the House.<ref>{{cite news|last1=Flahive|first1=Brad|title=Chloe Swarbrick set to become New Zealand's youngest MP in 42 years|url=https://www.stuff.co.nz/national/politics/97175081/new-zealands-youngest-mp-in-42-years|access-date=28 September 2017|publisher=[[Stuff (website)|Stuff]] |date=24 September 2017}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|title=Meet Golriz Ghahraman, the Green Party's newest Member of Parliament|url=http://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/news/article.cfm?c_id=1&objectid=11898165|access-date=7 October 2017|work=[[The New Zealand Herald]]|date=7 October 2017}}</ref>

Following the election results, Party Leader Shaw stated that the Greens would not be seeking a coalition with the National Party. He added that the party was pursuing a coalition rather than a support agreement with the Labour and socially-conservative New Zealand First parties.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Davison |first1=Isaac |title=Green Party leader James Shaw rules out contacting National|url=http://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/news/article.cfm?c_id=1&objectid=11925905 |access-date=28 September 2017|work=[[The New Zealand Herald]]|date=24 September 2017}}</ref> On 9 October, the Greens leader Shaw took part in negotiations with the Labour Party.<ref>{{cite news|title='I know it's frustrating'- James Shaw leaves media without answers following Labour talks|url=https://www.tvnz.co.nz/one-news/new-zealand/know-its-frustrating-james-shaw-leaves-media-without-answers-following-labour-talks|access-date=12 October 2017|publisher=[[1News]]|date=9 October 2017}}</ref>
During the coalition-forming negotiations, NZ First leader Peters turned down Shaw's invitation for the two parties to negotiate directly on the grounds that the Greens and Labour had campaigned together under a memorandum of understanding during the 2017 election.<ref>{{cite news|last1=Chang|first1=Derek|title=Winston Peters dismisses idea of meeting with Greens|url=http://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/news/article.cfm?c_id=1&objectid=11931588|access-date=12 October 2017|date=10 October 2017}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|title=Rub of the Greens: Winston Peters heaps scorn on Labour's partner|url=http://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/news/article.cfm?c_id=1&objectid=11931941|access-date=11 October 2017|work= [[The New Zealand Herald]]|date=11 October 2017}}</ref>

=== First term in Government (2017–2020) ===
{{Main|Sixth Labour Government of New Zealand}}

In October 2017, the Greens entered a confidence and supply arrangement with the Labour Party which gave them three ministers outside cabinet and one under-secretary role.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Phipps |first1=Claire |title=Jacinda Ardern is next prime minister of New Zealand, Winston Peters confirms – as it happened |url=https://www.theguardian.com/world/live/2017/oct/19/new-zealand-election-winston-peters-prime-minister-bill-english-jacinda-ardern-live?page=with:block-59e85c48389e4906e8cf9587#block-59e85c48389e4906e8cf9587 |access-date=1 September 2020 |work=[[The Guardian]] |date=19 October 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200901100442/https://www.theguardian.com/world/live/2017/oct/19/new-zealand-election-winston-peters-prime-minister-bill-english-jacinda-ardern-live?page=with%3Ablock-59e85c48389e4906e8cf9587%23block-59e85c48389e4906e8cf9587 |archive-date=1 September 2020|url-status=live}}</ref> This marked the first time the Greens had been in government.<ref>{{cite news|last1=Roy|first1=Eleanor Ainge|title=Jacinda Ardern to be New Zealand's next PM after Labour coalition deal|url=https://www.theguardian.com/world/2017/oct/19/jacinda-ardern-new-zealand-prime-minister-labour-coalition-deal-winston-peters|work=[[The Guardian]]|access-date=20 October 2017|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200812172425/https://www.theguardian.com/world/2017/oct/19/jacinda-ardern-new-zealand-prime-minister-labour-coalition-deal-winston-peters|archive-date=12 August 2020}}</ref> Party leader James Shaw was appointed Minister for Climate Change and Statistics and Associate Minister of Finance. [[Julie Anne Genter]] was made [[Ministry for Women|Minister for Women]] and Associate Minister of Health and Transport. [[Eugenie Sage]] was made Minister of Conservation and Land Information and Associate Minister for the Environment. [[Jan Logie]] was appointed Parliamentary Undersecretary to the [[Minister of Justice (New Zealand)|Minister of Justice]] with a focus on domestic and sexual violence issues.<ref>{{cite web|title=Ministerial List|url=https://www.dpmc.govt.nz/our-business-units/cabinet-office/ministers-and-their-portfolios/ministerial-list|publisher=[[Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet (New Zealand)|Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet]]|access-date=26 October 2017|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171129201736/https://dpmc.govt.nz/our-business-units/cabinet-office/ministers-and-their-portfolios/ministerial-list|archive-date=29 November 2017}}</ref>

As a support partner of the [[Sixth Labour Government of New Zealand|Labour-New Zealand First coalition government]], the Greens secured several policies and concessions including a proposed [[Climate Change Response (Zero Carbon) Amendment Act|Zero Carbon Act]], a [[2020 New Zealand cannabis referendum|referendum on legalising personal cannabis use]] by 2020, establishing a proposed [[Interim Climate Change Committee|Climate Commission]], a proposed [[Green Transport Card]] to reduce public transportation costs, investing in rail and cycle infrastructure, light rail construction to [[Auckland Airport]], increasing the [[Department of Conservation (New Zealand)|Department of Conservation]]'s funding, eliminating "excessive" benefit sanctions and the [[gender pay gap]], a rent-to-own-scheme as part of [[KiwiBuild]], and re-establishing the [[Mental Health Commission]].<ref>{{cite news|title=NZ First, Green Party, Labour coalition deals revealed|url=https://www.stuff.co.nz/national/politics/98170259/nz-prime-minister-elect-jacinda-ardern-reveals-cost-of-coalition|access-date=4 November 2017|work=[[Stuff (website)|Stuff]]|date=24 October 2017|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200809043742/https://www.stuff.co.nz/national/politics/98170259/nz-prime-minister-elect-jacinda-ardern-reveals-cost-of-coalition|archive-date=9 August 2020}}</ref>

In 2019, a number of Trans members resigned after a Green Party magazine published an article from a member concerned about the growing divide between women in the party and LGBTQIA+ members.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/greens-members-leave-after-transphobic-article-in-magazine/IANJW2LKDP5K6JMHCN64JXGAAI/|title=Greens members leave after 'transphobic' article in magazine|newspaper=[[New Zealand Herald]] |first=Boris|last=Jancic|date=3 September 2019}}</ref>

In late August 2020, Shaw was criticised by members of the Green Party, the opposition [[New Zealand National Party|National Party]], school principals and teachers unions for allocating, in his role as Associate Minister of Finance, NZ$11.7&nbsp;million from the Government's $3&nbsp;billion COVID-19 "shovel-ready" recovery fund to the private "Green School New Zealand" in [[Taranaki]]. This funding boost contradicted the party's own policy of opposing giving government funds to private schools. Shaw had lobbied for the inclusion of the school in the "shovel-ready" fund, claiming that it would have boosted the local economy and created jobs. 
Former Green MPs [[Catherine Delahunty]], [[Mojo Mathers]] and [[Sue Bradford]] denounced Shaw's decision as a betrayal of the Green Party's policies and principles.<ref>{{cite news |last1=McCulloch |first1=Craig |title=Critics pile on Green private school funding boost |url=https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/424605/critics-pile-on-green-private-school-funding-boost |access-date=27 August 2020 |work=[[Radio New Zealand]] |date=27 August 2020|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200827121626/https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/424605/critics-pile-on-green-private-school-funding-boost|archive-date=27 August 2020}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |last1=Coughlan |first1=Thomas |title=Greens caught bending party policy to grant $11.7m to private school in Taranaki |url=https://www.stuff.co.nz/national/politics/300092266/greens-caught-bending-party-policy-to-grant-117m-to-private-school-in-taranaki |access-date=27 August 2020 |work=[[Stuff (website)|Stuff]] |date=27 August 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200827121829/https://www.stuff.co.nz/national/politics/300092266/greens-caught-bending-party-policy-to-grant-117m-to-private-school-in-taranaki |archive-date=27 August 2020|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |last1=Collins |first1=Benedict |title=Widespread dismay at Government funding for elite Green School |url=https://www.tvnz.co.nz/one-news/new-zealand/widespread-dismay-government-funding-elite-green-school |access-date=27 August 2020 |work=[[1News]] |date=27 August 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200827122122/https://www.tvnz.co.nz/one-news/new-zealand/widespread-dismay-government-funding-elite-green-school |archive-date=27 August 2020|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |title=Green co-leader James Shaw refused to sign-off on $3bn of infrastructure projects unless Green School was included |url=https://www.newshub.co.nz/home/politics/2020/09/green-co-leader-james-shaw-refused-to-sign-off-on-3bn-of-infrastructure-projects-unless-green-school-was-included.html |access-date=1 September 2020 |work=[[Newshub]] |date=1 September 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200901094928/https://www.newshub.co.nz/home/politics/2020/09/green-co-leader-james-shaw-refused-to-sign-off-on-3bn-of-infrastructure-projects-unless-green-school-was-included.html |archive-date=1 September 2020|url-status=dead}}</ref> Shaw subsequently apologised to Green MPs during a [[Zoom (software)|Zoom]] call, describing his action as an "error of judgment."<ref>{{cite news |title=Green Party co-leader James Shaw apologises for 'error of judgement' over Green School funding |url=https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/424944/green-party-co-leader-james-shaw-apologises-for-error-of-judgement-over-green-school-funding |access-date=1 September 2020 |work=[[Radio New Zealand]] |date=1 September 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200901040530/https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/424944/green-party-co-leader-james-shaw-apologises-for-error-of-judgement-over-green-school-funding |archive-date=1 September 2020|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |last1=Coughlan |first1=Thomas |title=James Shaw calls Green School funding 'an error of judgment' as he searches for a solution |url=https://www.stuff.co.nz/national/politics/300096758/james-shaw-calls-green-school-funding-an-error-of-judgment-as-he-searches-for-a-solution |access-date=1 September 2020 |work=[[Stuff (website)|Stuff]] |date=1 September 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200901040810/https://www.stuff.co.nz/national/politics/300096758/james-shaw-calls-green-school-funding-an-error-of-judgment-as-he-searches-for-a-solution |archive-date=1 September 2020|url-status=live}}</ref> On 2 November, it was reported that the Government had reached an agreement with the school's owners, Michael and Rachel Perrett, for the NZ$11.7&nbsp;million grant to be converted into a loan; a development that was welcomed by local principals.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Coster |first1=Deena |last2=Harvey |first2=Helen |title=Taranaki principals happy Green School funding will be 100 per cent loan |url=https://www.stuff.co.nz/taranaki-daily-news/news/123266353/taranaki-principals-happy-green-school-funding-will-be-100-per-cent-loan |access-date=2 November 2020 |work=[[Taranaki Daily News]] |publisher=[[Stuff (website)|Stuff]] |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201102233536/https://www.stuff.co.nz/taranaki-daily-news/news/123266353/taranaki-principals-happy-green-school-funding-will-be-100-per-cent-loan |archive-date=2 November 2020|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |title=Green school's $11.7 million grant now a 100 per cent Government loan |url=https://www.tvnz.co.nz/one-news/new-zealand/green-schools-11-7-million-grant-now-100-per-cent-government-loan |access-date=2 November 2020 |work=[[1News]] |date=2 November 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201102233709/https://www.tvnz.co.nz/one-news/new-zealand/green-schools-11-7-million-grant-now-100-per-cent-government-loan |archive-date=2 November 2020|url-status=live}}</ref>

====2020 election====
[[File:The caucus of the Green Party of Aotearoa, New Zealand, 53rd Parliament.jpg|thumb|upright=1.4|The Green Party [[caucus]], 2020]]
During the [[2020 New Zealand general election]] held on 17 October, the Greens returned to Parliament with 7.9% of the popular vote, giving them ten seats. In addition, Green MP [[Chlöe Swarbrick]] won the [[Auckland Central (New Zealand electorate)|Auckland Central]] electorate seat by 1,068 votes.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Taylor |first1=Phil |title='We made history': New Zealand Greens on the rise after voters return to the fold |url=https://www.theguardian.com/world/2020/oct/18/greens-in-party-mode-after-strong-showing-in-new-zealand-election |access-date=19 October 2020 |work=[[The Guardian]] |date=18 October 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201019023222/https://www.theguardian.com/world/2020/oct/18/greens-in-party-mode-after-strong-showing-in-new-zealand-election |archive-date=19 October 2020|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |last1=Coughlan |first1=Thomas |title=Election 2020: Coming-of-age moment as Greens make MMP history |url=https://www.stuff.co.nz/national/politics/300131377/election-2020-comingofage-moment-as-greens-make-mmp-history |access-date=19 October 2020 |work=[[Stuff (website)|Stuff]] |date=18 October 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201019043415/https://www.stuff.co.nz/national/politics/300131377/election-2020-comingofage-moment-as-greens-make-mmp-history |archive-date=19 October 2020|url-status=live}}</ref><ref name="results2020">{{cite web|date=6 November 2020|title=2020 General Election and Referendums – Official Result|url= https://electionresults.govt.nz/electionresults_2020/|archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20230621001306/https://www.electionresults.govt.nz/electionresults_2020/|url-status= dead|archive-date= 21 June 2023|access-date=6 November 2020|website=Electoral Commission}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title=Auckland Central – Official Result|url=https://electionresults.govt.nz/electionresults_2020/electorate-details-01.html|access-date=6 November 2020|website=Electoral Commission}}</ref>

Despite the Labour Party winning a parliamentary majority and not needing to form a coalition agreement with other parties, Labour and the Green parties undertook a series of discussions about areas of cooperation.<ref>{{Cite news|title='Krispies on the table' – Green Party co-leader describes 'fruitful' discussion with Labour|language=en-NZ|work=TVNZ|url=https://www.tvnz.co.nz/one-news/new-zealand/krispies-table-green-party-co-leader-describes-fruitful-discussion-labour|access-date=31 October 2020}}</ref> Green co-leader James Shaw had indicated that the Greens would be open to negotiating with Labour about its [[wealth tax]] policy as part of coalition negotiations.<ref>{{cite news |title=Greens don't rule out bringing wealth tax policy to negotiation table in potential coalition with Labour |url=https://www.tvnz.co.nz/one-news/new-zealand/greens-dont-rule-bringing-wealth-tax-policy-negotiation-table-in-potential-coalition-labour |access-date=20 October 2020 |work=[[1News]] |date=18 October 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201020120004/https://www.tvnz.co.nz/one-news/new-zealand/greens-dont-rule-bringing-wealth-tax-policy-negotiation-table-in-potential-coalition-labour |archive-date=20 October 2020|url-status=live}}</ref> Earlier, Prime Minister Jacinda Ardern had ruled out supporting the Green's wealth tax policy during campaigning.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Trevett |first1=Claire |title=Election 2020: Jacinda Ardern rules out wealth tax while Prime Minister |url=https://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/election-2020-jacinda-ardern-rules-out-wealth-tax-while-prime-minister/72EAXTY2JKP4K4X6MEPAGHPSDM/ |access-date=20 October 2020 |work=[[The New Zealand Herald]] |date=14 October 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201015163405/https://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/election-2020-jacinda-ardern-rules-out-wealth-tax-while-prime-minister/72EAXTY2JKP4K4X6MEPAGHPSDM/ |archive-date=15 October 2020|url-status=live}}</ref> On 20 October, ''[[Newshub]]'' reported that Ardern was not seeking a formal coalition between Labour and the Green Party but was exploring a 2020|url-status=dead}}</ref>

=== Second term in Government (2020–2023) ===
Following prolonged negotiations between the Green and [[New Zealand Labour Party|Labour]] parties' leaderships, the Green Party accepted a deal on 31 October under which their co-leaders James Shaw and [[Marama Davidson]] would become ministers outside the Cabinet. Under this cooperation agreement, Shaw would remain Minister for Climate Change and become an associate minister for the environment (with responsibility for biodiversity) while Davidson would take the new role of Minister for the Prevention of Family and Sexual Violence and become an associate minister of housing (with responsibility for homelessness). In addition, Green MPs would fill one chair and one deputy chair role on two [[New Zealand House of Representatives committees|select committees]]. ''[[Stuff (website)|Stuff]]'' reported that these would likely be held by former ministers Eugenie Sage and Julie Anne Genter on the Environment Committee and Transport Committee, respectively.<ref>{{Cite news|date=31 October 2020|title=Election 2020: Green Party votes to be part of next Government with Labour |url=https://www.stuff.co.nz/national/politics/300146558/election-2020-green-party-votes-to-be-part-of-next-government-with-labour|access-date=31 October 2020 |website=[[Stuff (website)|Stuff]] |language=en|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201102070727/https://www.stuff.co.nz/national/politics/300146558/election-2020-green-party-votes-to-be-part-of-next-government-with-labour|archive-date=2 November 2020|url-status=live}}</ref> During a [[Zoom (software)|Zoom]] call, 85% of the 150 Green Party delegates voted to accept this cooperation agreement with Labour.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Coughlan |first1=Thomas |last2=Cooke |first2=Henry |title=Election 2020: Green Party votes to be part of next Government with Labour |url=https://www.stuff.co.nz/national/politics/300146558/election-2020-green-party-votes-to-be-part-of-next-government-with-labour?cid=app-iPhone |access-date=31 October 2020 |work=[[Stuff (website)|Stuff]] |date=31 October 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201031095900/https://www.stuff.co.nz/national/politics/300146558/election-2020-green-party-votes-to-be-part-of-next-government-with-labour?cid=app-iPhone |archive-date=31 October 2020|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |title=Greens accept Labour's offer for 'cooperation agreement' |url=https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/429559/greens-accept-labour-s-offer-for-cooperation-agreement |access-date=31 October 2020 |work=[[Radio New Zealand]] |date=31 October 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201031101638/https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/429559/greens-accept-labour-s-offer-for-cooperation-agreement |archive-date=31 October 2020|url-status=live}}</ref>

The agreement was described by Ardern as "honouring the mandate provided to Labour to form a majority Government in our own right" while ensuring the Government "govern[s] for all New Zealanders and to reach as wide a consensus on key issues as possible."<ref>{{Cite news|title=Jacinda Ardern on giving Greens post-election deal despite Labour majority: 'I wanted to govern for all New Zealanders'|language=en|work=[[Newshub]]|url=https://www.newshub.co.nz/home/politics/2020/10/jacinda-ardern-on-giving-greens-post-election-deal-despite-labour-majority-i-wanted-to-govern-for-all-new-zealanders.html|access-date=31 October 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201102071117/https://www.newshub.co.nz/home/politics/2020/10/jacinda-ardern-on-giving-greens-post-election-deal-despite-labour-majority-i-wanted-to-govern-for-all-new-zealanders.html|archive-date=2 November 2020}}</ref> Several former Green MPs, including former co-leader [[Russel Norman]], [[Sue Bradford]], and [[Catherine Delahunty]], criticised the cooperation agreement for giving the Greens a weak position to influence the policy process within the newly formed Labour Government.<ref>{{cite news |title=Former Greens MPs express disappointment about party's deal with Labour |url=https://www.tvnz.co.nz/one-news/new-zealand/former-greens-mps-including-co-leader-express-disappointment-partys-deal-labour |access-date=2 November 2020 |work=[[1News]] |date=1 November 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201102071447/https://www.tvnz.co.nz/one-news/new-zealand/former-greens-mps-including-co-leader-express-disappointment-partys-deal-labour |archive-date=2 November 2020|url-status=live}}</ref>

On 19 May, Ghahraman sponsored a motion on behalf of the Green Party calling for Members of Parliament to recognise the right of Palestinians to self-determination and statehood. The motion was supported by the Greens and the [[Māori Party]] but was opposed by the centre-right [[New Zealand National Party|National]] and [[ACT New Zealand|ACT]] parties. The governing Labour Party also declined to support the Greens' motion, with the Speaker of the House [[Trevor Mallard]] criticising Ghahraman for sponsoring the motion despite knowing that it was going to be voted down.<ref>{{cite news |title= Green Party motion to call for recognition of Palestine's right to self-determination |url=https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/442887/green-party-motion-to-call-for-recognition-of-palestine-s-right-to-self-determination |access-date=21 May 2021 |work=[[Radio New Zealand]] |date=19 May 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210520003402/https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/442887/green-party-motion-to-call-for-recognition-of-palestine-s-right-to-self-determination |archive-date=20 May 2021|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |last1=Manch |first1=Thomas |title=Green Party's motion to declare Palestine a state fails in Parliament |url=https://www.stuff.co.nz/national/politics/125175638/green-partys-motion-to-declare-palestine-a-state-fails-in-parliament |access-date=21 May 2021 |work=[[Stuff (website)|Stuff]] |date=19 May 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210520053549/https://www.stuff.co.nz/national/politics/125175638/green-partys-motion-to-declare-palestine-a-state-fails-in-parliament |archive-date=20 May 2021|url-status=live}}</ref>

In June 2021, it was revealed the Green Party had received $54,000 in donations from Lindsay Fraser, whom the [[Royal New Zealand Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals]] (RNZSPCA) has called the worst animal abuser in New Zealand history.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.newsroom.co.nz/greens-wont-be-returning-54k-donations-from-animal-abuser|title=Greens won't be returning $54k donations from animal abuser|publisher=Newsroom|first=Pete|last=McKenzie|date=8 June 2021}}</ref>

In July 2021, Shaw's [[2021 Green Party of Aotearoa New Zealand male co-leadership election|co-leadership of the Greens was challenged]] by Dunedin climate activist and software developer James Cockle, who expressed dissatisfaction that the Greens were being seen as "Labour's little helper."<ref>{{cite news |first=Katie |last=Scotcher |url=https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/446311/green-party-leadership-challenge-james-shaw-vs-james-cockle |title=Green Party leadership challenge: James Shaw vs James Cockle |work=[[Radio New Zealand]] |date=6 July 2021 |accessdate=8 August 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210808023751/https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/446311/green-party-leadership-challenge-james-shaw-vs-james-cockle|archive-date=8 August 2021|url-status=live}}</ref> During a vote at the party's annual general meeting in August 2021, Shaw was overwhelmingly re-elected, winning 116 delegate votes with just four to Cockle.<ref>{{cite news |url=https://www.stuff.co.nz/national/300377436/greens-coleader-james-shaw-easily-beats-off-challenge |title=Greens co-leader James Shaw easily beats off challenge |work=[[Stuff (website)|Stuff]] |date=7 August 2021 |accessdate=8 August 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210808023744/https://www.stuff.co.nz/national/300377436/greens-coleader-james-shaw-easily-beats-off-challenge|archive-date=8 August 2021|url-status=live}}</ref>

In January 2022, [[Radio New Zealand]] reported that several Green Party executive and policy branch members had resigned from the Party citing disagreement with the Green Party leadership's cooperation agreement with the governing Labour Party, taking issue with what they regarded as the Greens' perceived limited ability to hold the Government to account on policy differences. These former members also alleged Shaw was practising an autocratic leadership style and that the party executive was not holding the parliamentary caucus and leadership to account over policy decisions in government. In addition, several former Green leaders and MPs, including Bradford, Delahunty, and Norman, criticised the party's limited position within the Labour Government, the Government's alleged pro-business policies, and climate change position.  In response to criticism, co-leaders Shaw and Davidson claimed that the party was democratic and making "progressive changes" in government.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Hall |first1=Michael |title=Green Party discontent: Members walk, ex-MPs criticise leadership |url=https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/459250/green-party-discontent-members-walk-ex-mps-criticise-leadership |access-date=28 January 2022 |work=[[Radio New Zealand]] |date=9 January 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220109172648/https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/459250/green-party-discontent-members-walk-ex-mps-criticise-leadership |archive-date=9 January 2022|url-status=live}}</ref>

In early May 2022, the Green Party scrapped its male co-leadership requirement during a weekend special meeting to amend its constitution. Under these changes, the two new co-leaders now need to consist of one woman and one person of any gender (with leadership pathways for [[non-binary]] and intersex individuals). In addition, at least one of the future co-leaders is required to be of [[Māori people|Māori]] descent.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Neilson |first1=Michael |title=Greens ditch male co-leader rule and add Māori requirement |url=https://www.newstalkzb.co.nz/news/politics/green-party-scraps-male-co-leader-requirement-adds-maori-as-part-of-te-tiriti-o-waitangi-commitment/ |access-date=3 May 2022 |work=[[Newstalk ZB]] |publisher=[[NZME]] |date=3 May 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220502225043/https://www.newstalkzb.co.nz/news/politics/green-party-scraps-male-co-leader-requirement-adds-maori-as-part-of-te-tiriti-o-waitangi-commitment/ |archive-date=2 May 2022|url-status=live}}</ref>

On 23 July, an annual general meeting was held online to decide on the party's leadership. While Davidson was re-elected unopposed, 32 of the 107 delegates voted to reopen nominations for Shaw's position, meeting the 25% threshold needed to remove him as co-leader and trigger [[2022 Green Party of Aotearoa New Zealand co-leadership election|a leadership election]] under the party's rules.<ref>{{cite news |first1=Tracy |last1=Watkins |first2=Jono |last2=Galuszka |url=https://www.stuff.co.nz/national/politics/300644340/surprised-james-shaw-not-reconfirmed-as-green-party-coleader-nominations-to-be-reopened |title=Surprised James Shaw not reconfirmed as Green Party co-leader, nominations to be reopened |work=[[Stuff (website)|Stuff]] |date=23 July 2022 |access-date=23 July 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220725230027/https://www.stuff.co.nz/national/politics/300644340/surprised-james-shaw-not-reconfirmed-as-green-party-coleader-nominations-to-be-reopened|archive-date=25 July 2022|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |first=Craig |last=McCulloch |url=https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/471489/green-party-s-james-shaw-to-face-leadership-challenge |title=Green |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220726105300/https://www.stuff.co.nz/national/politics/129367235/green-party-leadership-and-james-shaw-what-you-need-to-know |archive-date=26 July 2022|url-status=live}}</ref> On 25 July, Shaw confirmed that he would contest the co-leadership election.<ref>{{cite news |first1=Luke |last1=Malpass |first2=Thomas |last2=Manch |url=https://www.stuff.co.nz/national/politics/300645122/james-shaw-confirms-he-will-recontest-greens-coleadership |title=James Shaw confirms he will recontest Greens co-leadership |website=[[Stuff July 2022 |title=Chloe Swarbrick rules out bid to be Greens co-leader |url=https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/471587/chloe-swarbrick-rules-out-bid-to-be-greens-co-leader |access-date=25 July 2022 |work=[[Radio New Zealand]] |language=en-nz |archive-date=25 July 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220725230027/https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/471587/chloe-swarbrick-rules-out-bid-to-be-greens-co-leader |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{Cite news
