}}</ref>

On 10 September, Shaw was re-elected as Green Party co-leader by 142 (97%) of the 145 eligible delegates in the party's special election. Shaw was the only candidate to contest the 2022 co-leadership election.<ref name="Shaw, September 2022">{{cite news |url=https://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/politics/james-shaw-re-elected-green-co-leader-six-weeks-after-ouster/SG4XUFT7JEC5P5IW2A2FEWXEMY/ |title=James Shaw re-elected Green co-leader six weeks after ouster |first=Thomas |last=Coughlan |work=[[The New Zealand Herald]] |date=10 September 2022 |accessdate=10 September 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220911112015/https://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/politics/james-shaw-re-elected-green-co-leader-six-weeks-after-ouster/SG4XUFT7JEC5P5IW2A2FEWXEMY/|archive-date=11 September 2022|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |url=https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/474500/james-shaw-re-elected-as-green-party-co-leader-by-delegates |title=James Shaw re-elected as Green Party co-leader by delegates |first=Katie |last=Scocher |publisher=[[Radio New Zealand]] |date=10 September 2022 |accessdate=10 September 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220911112326/https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/474500/james-shaw-re-elected-as-green-party-co-leader-by-delegates|archive-date=11 September 2022|url-status=live }}</ref>

====2023 election====
As part of the party's policy plan for the [[2023 New Zealand general election|2023 general election]] it put forward the policy of a guaranteed minimum income for those out of work and those studying of [[New Zealand dollar|$]]385 a week for individuals, $770 a week for couples, and $735 for single parents, all after tax. This would be phased in over 2 years and paid for via a wealth tax of 2.5% (two point five percent) on assets worth more than four million New Zealand dollars for couples and two million for singles, as well as a top rate of tax of 45% on incomes over $180,000 and a 33% corporate tax rate. Those with a salary under $125,000 would be granted a tax free threshold of $10,000.<ref>{{cite news |date= 11 June 2023 |title= Green's tax plan could 'end child poverty' – Shaw |url= https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5tIGUt-Aa2Y |work= YouTube |publisher=[[1News]] |access-date= 7 December 2023}}</ref> The party stated this would result in "tax cuts of between $16 and $26 a week for 3.7 million New Zealanders" and anyone earning under $125,000 would pay less tax as part of its plan.<ref>{{cite web |url= https://www.greens.org.nz/green_party_s_new_income_guarantee_for_every_new_zealander |title= Green Party's new Income Guarantee for every New Zealander |last1= Shaw |first1= James |last2= Davidson |first2= Marama |date= 11 June 2023 |website= greens.org.nz |publisher= Green Party of Aotearoa New Zealand |access-date= 7 December 2023}}</ref>

In the 2023 general election, the Green Party's share of the party vote rose to 11.6% and it increased its number of seats by six to 15: three electorates and 12 list MPs. This is the highest number of Green MPs to ever be elected into Parliament thus far.<ref>{{cite web |title=Official count – Overall Results |url=https://electionresults.govt.nz/electionresults_2023/ |publisher=[[Electoral Commission (New Zealand)|Electoral Commission]] |access-date=20 November 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231107112928/https://www.electionresults.govt.nz/electionresults_2023/ |archive-date=7 November 2023 |date=3 November 2023 |url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=2023 General Election: Successful candidates |url=https://electionresults.govt.nz/electionresults_2023/successful-candidates.html |publisher=[[Electoral Commission (New Zealand)|Electoral Commission]] |access-date=20 November 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231117114239/https://electionresults.govt.nz/electionresults_2023/successful-candidates.html |archive-date=17 November 2023 |date=3 November 2023 |url-status=live}}</ref>  The party returned to opposition, as support partner Labour came second to National.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Hatton |first1=Emma |title=Bittersweet election night wins for Greens |url=https://www.newsroom.co.nz/bittersweet-election-night-wins-for-greens |access-date=17 October 2023 |work=[[Newsroom (website)|Newsroom]] |date=15 October 2023 |language=en-AU}}</ref>

=== In opposition (2023–present) ===
In January 2024 Shaw announced that he would be resigning as co-leader of the Green Party and retiring from politics.<ref name="2024resignation">{{cite web |last1=Shaw |first1=James |title=James Shaw announces resignation |url=https://www.greens.org.nz/james_shaw_announces_resignation |publisher=Green Party of Aotearoa New Zealand |access-date=2 February 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240130104650/https://www.greens.org.nz/james_shaw_announces_resignation |archive-date=30 January 2024 |date=24 January 2024}}</ref><ref name="2024resignationstuff">{{cite news|first1=Glenn|last1=McConnell|title=James Shaw steps down as Green co-leader, to ease out of politics|language=en|work=[[Stuff (website)|Stuff]]|date=29 January 2024|access-date=29 January 2024|url=https://www.stuff.co.nz/politics/350162174/james-shaw-steps-down-green-co-leader-ease-out-politics|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240129231122/https://www.stuff.co.nz/politics/350162174/james-shaw-steps-down-green-co-leader-ease-out-politics|archive-date=29 January 2024|url-status=live}}</ref> Amid shoplifting allegations, Golriz Ghahraman resigned in January 2024. She was replaced by Celia Wade-Brown.<ref>{{cite web|title= Golriz Ghahraman resigns from Parliament after shoplifting allegations|website= [[Radio New Zealand]]|date= 16 January 2024|url= https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/506825/golriz-ghahraman-resigns-from-parliament-after-shoplifting-allegations}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|title= Former Wellington mayor Celia Wade-Brown stepping in to replace Ghahraman|url= https://www.thepost.co.nz/nz-news/350149238/former-wellington-mayor-celia-wade-brown-stepping-replace-ghahraman}}</ref> On 21 February 2024, Fa'anānā [[Efeso Collins]] died during a charity run in Auckland.<ref>{{cite web|title=Green MP Efeso Collins dies during charity run |website= [[Radio New Zealand]]|date= 21 February 2024|url= https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/509745/green-mp-efeso-collins-dies-during-charity-run}}</ref> He was replaced by [[Lawrence Xu-Nan]].<ref>{{cite news |url=https://www.stuff.co.nz/nz-news/350188432/faanana-efeso-collins-death-brings-another-new-green-mp-parliament |title=Fa'anānā Efeso Collins' death brings another new Green MP to Parliament |date=22 February 2024 |work=[[Stuff (website)|Stuff]] |access-date=6 March 2024}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |title=Declaration by Electoral Commission that Lawrence Xi Xu-Nan is elected a Member of Parliament |date=6 March 2024 |work=[[New Zealand Gazette]] |url=https://gazette.govt.nz/notice/id/2024-au985 |access-date=6 March 2024}}</ref> On 15 March 2024, [[Darleen Tana]] was stood down after allegations of migrant exploitation.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.stuff.co.nz/nz-news/350212641/bike-shop-green-mp-and-alleged-migrant-exploitation|title=The bike shop, the Green MP, and alleged migrant exploitation|publisher=[[Stuff (website)|Stuff]] |first=Steve|last=Kilgallon|date=15 March 2024}}</ref> On 6 May 2024, James Shaw resigned from parliament and was replaced by [[Francisco Hernandez (politician)|Francisco Hernandez]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Declaration by Electoral Commission That Francisco Bagkus Hernandez is Elected a Member of Parliament – 2024-au2073 – New Zealand Gazette |url=https://gazette.govt.nz/notice/id/2024-au2073 |access-date=16 May 2024 |website=gazette.govt.nz}}</ref> In late September 2024, Swarbrick announced that the Greens would hold a special meeting on 17 October to decide whether to expel Tana from Parliament using the waka-jumping legislation.<ref>{{cite news |title=Greens reschedule waka-jumping decision on Darleen Tana |url=https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/528873/greens-reschedule-waka-jumping-decision-on-darleen-tana |access-date=27 September 2024 |work=[[RNZ]] |date=24 September 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240925185224/https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/528873/greens-reschedule-waka-jumping-decision-on-darleen-tana |archive-date=25 September 2024|url-status=live}}</ref> In mid-October, Tana appealed the High Court ruling upholding the Green Party's proceedings to expel her from Parliament. In response, Swarbrick said that the appeal would not affect the special meeting scheduled for 17 October.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Coughlan |first1=Thomas |title=Darleen Tana appeals, but Greens continue process to oust her |url=https://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/politics/darleen-tana-appeals-but-greens-continue-process-to-oust-her/USM7NP5YYJCQBASDDZFPOGD6MI/ |access-date=20 October 2024 |work=[[The New Zealand Herald]] |date=15 October 2024}}</ref> At that meeting 185 party delegates voted to support the use of the legislation by an overwhelming consensus.<ref>{{citation|title=Waka-jumping law: Green Party meets to decide former Green MP Darleen Tana's fate|language=en|work=[[The New Zealand Herald]] |first1=Thomas|last1=Coughlan|date=17 October 2024|access-date=17 October 2024|url=https://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/politics/waka-jumping-law-green-party-meets-to-decide-former-green-mp-darleen-tanas-fate/H5FGWH72AFH5FDK4IDUAYOBPQA/}}</ref> On 22 October, House Speaker [[Gerry Brownlee]] revoked Tana's ability to attend Parliament and expelled her using the [[Electoral (Integrity) Amendment Acts#Electoral (Integrity) Amendment Act 2018|Electoral (Integrity) Amendment Act 2018]]. She ceased to be an MP immediately following this announcement.<ref>{{cite news |last1=McConnell |first1=Glenn|title=As Darleen Tana booted from Parliament, Greens seek to move on |url=https://www.stuff.co.nz/politics/360459754/darleen-tana-booted-parliament-greens-seek-move |access-date=22 October 2024 |work=[[Stuff (website)|Stuff]] |date=22 October 2024}}</ref> In response to the ruling, Tana maintained her innocence but said she respected the speaker's decision due to the waka-jumping law.<ref>{{cite news |title=Exclusive: Darleen Tana says she's relieved to leave Parliament |url=https://www.1news.co.nz/2024/10/22/exclusive-darleen-tana-says-shes-relieved-to-leave-parliament/ |access-date=23 October 2024 |work=[[1News]] |date=22 October 2024}}</ref> [[Benjamin Doyle]] entered Parliament in November 2024 following the removal of [[Darleen Tana]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Declaration by Electoral Commission That Benjamin Cody Doyle is Elected a Member of Parliament – 2024-au5458- New Zealand Gazette |url=https://gazette.govt.nz/notice/id/2024-au5458 |access-date=26 May 2025 |website=gazette.govt.nz}}</ref> 

In early November 2024, the Greens' Copyright (Parody and Satire) Amendment Bill, which proposed allowing copyrighted works to be used for parody, satire and [[meme]]s, was pulled from Parliament's ballot.<ref>{{cite news |title=Greens' Copyright (Parody and Satire) bill to be debated in Parliament |url=https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/533216/greens-copyright-parody-and-satire-bill-to-be-debated-in-parliament |access-date=11 November 2024 |work=[[RNZ]] |date=8 November 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241111011239/https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/533216/greens-copyright-parody-and-satire-bill-to-be-debated-in-parliament |archive-date=11 November 2024}}</ref> On 20 November, Green MP [[Teanau Tuiono]]'s [[Citizenship (Western Samoa) (Restoration) Amendment Act 2024|member's bill]] restoring [[New Zealand citizenship]] to people born in [[Western Samoa]] between 1924 and 1949 passed into law with unanimous support from all parties.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Tinetali-Fiavaai |first1=Grace |title='685's to the world:' Restoring Citizenship Bill passes with unanimous support |url=https://www.rnz.co.nz/international/pacific-news/534339/685-s-to-the-world-restoring-citizenship-bill-passes-with-unanimous-support |access-date=20 November 2024 |work=[[RNZ]] |date=20 November 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241120085644/https://www.rnz.co.nz/international/pacific-news/534339/685-s-to-the-world-restoring-citizenship-bill-passes-with-unanimous-support|archive-date=20 November 2024|url-status=live}}</ref>

In early May 2025, Swarbrick unveiled the Greens' alternative budget, which proposed investing $8 billion over the next four years in various green policies including creating a Ministry of Green Works and supporting sustainable infrastructure.<ref>{{cite news |title=Green Party unveils new scheme promising to create thousands of 'green jobs' |url=https://www.newstalkzb.co.nz/on-air/heather-du-plessis-allan-drive/audio/chloee-swarbrick-green-party-co-leader-on-the-partys-plan-to-create-thousands-of-green-jobs/ |access-date=1 May 2025 |work=[[Newstalk ZB]] |date=1 May 2025 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250501225606/https://www.newstalkzb.co.nz/on-air/heather-du-plessis-allan-drive/audio/chloee-swarbrick-green-party-co-leader-on-the-partys-plan-to-create-thousands-of-green-jobs/ |archive-date=1 May 2025 |url-status=live}}</ref> Other key Green Budget policies have included a new [[wealth tax]], higher corporate taxes, a private jet tax, higher mining royalties and income tax rates.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Daalder |first1=Marc |title=Greens try to set agenda on pre-Budget tax debate |url=https://newsroom.co.nz/2025/05/20/greens-try-to-set-agenda-on-pre-budget-tax-debate/ |access-date=24 May 2025 |work=[[Newsroom (website)|Newsroom]] |date=20 May 2025 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250519215336/https://newsroom.co.nz/2025/05/20/greens-try-to-set-agenda-on-pre-budget-tax-debate/ |archive-date=19 May 2025 |url-status=live}}</ref> In response, the ACT party described the Green Budget as a "reckless attack on family farming" while Prime Minister Luxon described the alternative budget as "clown show economics." On 18 May, Swarbrick defended the Green Budget as during an interview with [[TVNZ]] journalist [[Jack Tame]], saying that it had been "independently costed."<ref>{{cite news |last1=Hun |first1=Justin |title='Not a gotcha': Swarbrick pushed on details over Green budget |url=https://www.1news.co.nz/2025/05/19/not-a-gotcha-swarbrick-pushed-on-details-over-green-budget/ |access-date=24 May 2025 |work=[[1News]] |date=18 May 2025}}</ref>

In mid July 2025, the Greens' supported the National-led coalition government's proposed online casino legislation during its first reading, which would introduce 15 licenses for online casinos operating in New Zealand.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Palmer |first1=Russell |title=Online casino bill: Greens vote with coalition govt to pass first reading |url=https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/566995/online-casino-bill-greens-vote-with-coalition-govt-to-pass-first-reading |access-date=20 July 2025 |work=[[RNZ]] |date=15 July 2025 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250716044649/https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/566995/online-casino-bill-greens-vote-with-coalition-govt-to-pass-first-reading |archive-date=16 July 2025 |url-status=live}}</ref> On 5 September 2025, [[Benjamin Doyle]] announced they would resign from Parliament, effective 3 October, citing safety concerns. [[Mike Davidson (politician)|Mike Davidson]] would enter Parliament to fill the vacancy.<ref>{{cite news |first1=Glenn |last1=McConnell |url=https://www.stuff.co.nz/politics/360815002/green-mp-benjamin-doyle-resigns-citing-safety-concerns |title=Green MP Benjamin Doyle resigns, citing safety concerns |access-date=5 September 2025 |date=5 September 2025 |work=[[Stuff (website)|Stuff]]}}</ref> In mid November 2025, co-leader Davidson announced that a Green government would revoke coal, gold and seabed mining consents approved under the National-led coalition government's [[Fast-track Approvals Act 2024]].<ref>{{cite news |last1=Gabel |first1=Julia |title='On notice': Green Party unveils mining policy ahead of 2026 general election |url=https://www.newstalkzb.co.nz/news/national/on-notice-green-party-unveils-mining-policy-ahead-of-2026-general-election/ |access-date=17 November 2025 |work=[[Newstalk ZB]] |date=17 November 2025 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20251117053812/https://www.newstalkzb.co.nz/news/national/on-notice-green-party-unveils-mining-policy-ahead-of-2026-general-election/ |archive-date=17 November 2025 |url-status=live}}</ref>

In response to fuel shortages in March 2026 caused by the [[2026 Iran war]], the Green Party offered to support the National-led coalition government's crisis-relief package in Parliament if the government agreed to subsidise free public transportation, transport relief payments for low income earners and rural residents, increase mileage rates for care and support workers and reverse cuts to school bus funding and the Total Mobility Scheme.<ref>{{cite news |last1=MacDuff |first1=Keller |title=Greens offer votes for National Party crisis-relief package in -with conditions |url=https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/590334/greens-offer-votes-for-national-party-crisis-relief-package-with-conditions |access-date=24 March 2026 |work=[[RNZ]] |date=23 March 2026 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260324031548/https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/590334/greens-offer-votes-for-national-party-crisis-relief-package-with-conditions |archive-date=24 March 2026 |url-status=live}}</ref> On 24 March, the Government announced its NZ$373 million relief package which consisted of a $50 in-work tax credit for 143,000 working families with children from 7 April, and a lower tax credit for another 14,000 families will also be eligible. While beneficiaries and pensioners would be ineligible for the tax credit, their payments would be adjusted from 1 April per procedure.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Pearse |first1=Adam |title=Fuel crisis: About 140,000 families to receive $50 a week to help with high fuel prices |url=https://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/politics/fuel-prices-government-to-announce-support-package-for-families-under-the-pump-as-petrol-hits-4-a-litre-in-some-areas/4IGEJBXRFZAUPOUCSWCB2ECOGA/ |access-date=24 March 2026 |work=[[The New Zealand Herald]] |date=24 March 2026 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260324035032/https://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/politics/fuel-prices-government-to-announce-support-package-for-families-under-the-pump-as-petrol-hits-4-a-litre-in-some-areas/4IGEJBXRFZAUPOUCSWCB2ECOGA/ |archive-date=24 March 2026 |url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |title=Fuel relief package: Who is eligible and how does it work? |url=https://www.1news.co.nz/2026/03/24/fuel-relief-package-who-is-eligible-and-how-does-it-work/ |access-date=24 March 2026 |work=[[1News]] |date=24 March 2026 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260324031918/https://www.1news.co.nz/2026/03/24/fuel-relief-package-who-is-eligible-and-how-does-it-work/ |archive-date=24 March 2026 |url-status=live}}</ref> In response, Swarbrick described the tax credits as insufficient for helping low income groups and said it favoured fossil fuels over public transportation.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Hu |first1=Justin |title='Fails to meet the crisis': Govt fuel relief draws opposition reaction |url=https://www.1news.co.nz/2026/03/24/fails-to-meet-the-crisis-govt-fuel-relief-draws-opposition-reaction/ |access-date=24 March 2026 |work=[[1News]] |date=24 March 2026 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260324031921/https://www.1news.co.nz/2026/03/24/fails-to-meet-the-crisis-govt-fuel-relief-draws-opposition-reaction/ |archive-date=24 March 2026 |url-status=live}}</ref>
==Ideology==
{{Green politics sidebar}}[[File:Green Party banner.jpg|thumb|Green Party supporters attending a demonstration in Christchurch on 1 December 2012]]

=== Green Party Charter ===
The party has four pillars like many [[green parties]] around the world; [[Ecosophy|ecological wisdom]], [[social justice]], [[grassroots democracy]], and [[nonviolence]].<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Kitschelt|first1=Herbert P.|s2cid=189889610|title=Review of The Global Promise of Green Politics|jstor=657226|journal=Theory and Society|pages=525–533|date=1 January 1985|volume=14 |issue=4 |doi=10.1007/BF00159254}}</ref> Internationally, it is affiliated with the [[Global Greens]]<ref name="globalgreens" /> whose common charter includes these. The party accepts the [[Treaty of Waitangi]] as the founding document of New Zealand and recognises Māori as ''[[tangata whenua]]'' ('people of the land').<ref>{{Cite web |title=Our Charter |url=https://www.greens.org.nz/charter |access-date=11 October 2026 |website=Green Party of Aotearoa New Zealand |language=en}}</ref> 

These charter princples have are read by most Greens as a connected programme despite much media and commentator suggesting an inherent tension between a focus on environmental and social issues. For example Nandor Tanzcos stated: "anyone who says that the Green party should stick to the environment fundamentally fails to understand what Green politics is by its very nature. The Greens aren’t the ‘environment party’, they’re the Green party," and that "Green politics has never been about preserving the environment, it’s always been about the relationships we have with each other and the rest of life on this planet."<ref>{{Cite web |title=Greens icon Nándor Tánczos on Metiria and what the party really stands for |url=https://thespinoff.co.nz/politics/11-08-2017/greens-icon-nandor-tanczos-on-metiria-and-what-the-party-really-stands-for |access-date=2026-10-13 |website=The Spinoff |language=en}}</ref>

The Greens rely heavily on the well-educated, urban demographic for their [[voter base]]. Green voters have various priorities but are likely to have a high regard for the environment and environmental issues. However, research indicates very few people who vote Green do so purely for environmental concerns.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Cowie |first1=Lucy J. |last2=Greaves |first2=Lara M. |last3=Sibley |first3=Chris G. |title=Identifying Distinct Subgroups of Green Voters: A Latent Profile Analysis of Crux Values Relating to Green Party Support |journal=New Zealand Journal of Psychology |date=March 2015 |volume=44 |issue=1 |url=https://www.psychology.org.nz/journal-archive/Article-51.pdf |access-date=12 November 2022 |publisher=University of Auckland |location=Auckland, New Zealand |issn=1179-7924}}</ref>

The charter has been open to various ideological interpretations with MPs such as Sue Bradford and Keith Locke<ref>{{Cite web |title=Keith Locke {{!}} Green Left |url=https://www.greenleft.org.au/content/keith-locke |access-date=2026-10-13 |website=www.greenleft.org.au}}</ref>, high profile former candidate and staffer Jack McDonald<ref>{{Cite web |last=Aotearoa |first=RNZ {{!}} Te Reo Irirangi o |date=4 August 2019 |title=High ranking Greens member pulls pin before election |url=https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/politics/395936/high-ranking-greens-member-pulls-pin-before-election |access-date=11 October 2026 |website=RNZ |language=en-nz}}</ref> believing this necessitates a eco-socialist vision, whereas others have argued it specifically excludes this. 2026 candidate Mike Finlayson describes himself as an ecosocialist.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Meet The Candidate: Mike Finlayson |url=https://tehiku.nz/p.Osn |access-date=11 October 2026 |website=Te Hiku Media |language=en}}</ref> In a 2012 book ''Beyond Tomorrow: A Values Story'', the author Claire Browning said the book "says one thing some members won’t like. The Greens are an ecological economic party, a party that puts the environment first, not a party of the Left – and a party that implicitly, in its first charter principle, stands for diversity and ''inclusion''."<ref>{{Cite web |title=Beyond Today: a values story, and the Greens' story {{!}} Pundit |url=http://pundit.co.nz/content/beyond-today-a-values-story-and-the-greens%E2%80%99-story |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130208193006/http://pundit.co.nz/content/beyond-today-a-values-story-and-the-greens%E2%80%99-story |archive-date=8 February 2013 |access-date=11 October 2026 |website=pundit.co.nz |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{cite web | title=An Interview with Claire Browning – Tim Jones | date=August 2012 | url=https://www.timjonesbooks.co.nz/2012/08/01/an-interview-with-claire-browning/ | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210116200402/https://www.timjonesbooks.co.nz/2012/08/01/an-interview-with-claire-browning/ | archive-date=16 January 2021 }}</ref><ref>{{cite web | title=Remarks on 40 years | date=2 June 2012 | url=http://pundit.co.nz/content/remarks-on-40-years | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130208192328/http://pundit.co.nz/content/remarks-on-40-years | archive-date=8 February 2013 }}</ref> Candidate Vernon Tava,<ref>{{Cite web |last=Tava |first=Vernon |date=24 September 2014 |title=Is the Green Party of the Left or is it a Party for Sustainability? |url=https://vernontava.com/2014/09/25/is-the-green-party-of-the-left-or-is-it-a-party-of-sustainability/ |access-date=11 October 2026 |website=Vernon Tava |language=en}}</ref> and MP Kennedy Graham,<ref>{{Cite web |title=Dr Kennedy Graham: Why green isn't just a shade of red |url=https://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/dr-kennedy-graham-why-green-isnt-just-a-shade-of-red/HDAYMXDBJJ25GY4ENYJYLLLNW4/ |access-date=11 October 2026 |website=NZ Herald |language=en-NZ}}</ref> agreed with this view.

==== Environment ====
The Greens have campaigned on a number of issues over time such as [[Mining in New Zealand|mining]] of [[National parks of New Zealand|national parks]],<ref>{{cite web |url=http://greens.org.nz/conservation/mining |title=NZ Greens Conservation Mining |publisher=Green Party of Aotearoa New Zealand |access-date=31 January 2011 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20101231083238/http://www.greens.org.nz/conservation/mining |archive-date=31 December 2010}}</ref> [[Water in New Zealand|fresh water]],<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.greens.org.nz/water|title=Campaigns: Water|publisher=Green Party of Aotearoa New Zealand|access-date=31 January 2011|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20101231001614/http://www.greens.org.nz/water|archive-date=31 December 2010}}</ref> [[peak oil]]<ref>{{cite web |url=http://greens.org.nz/campaigns/peakoil/ |title=NZ Greens: Campaigns: Peak Oil |publisher=Green Party of Aotearoa New Zealand |access-date=29 June 2008 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080704070931/http://www.greens.org.nz/campaigns/peakoil/ |archive-date=4 July 2008}}</ref> and the release of [[genetic engineering|genetically engineered]] organisms.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://greens.org.nz/ge/ |title=NZ Greens: Campaigns: Genetic Engineering |publisher=Green Party of Aotearoa New Zealand |access-date=29 June 2008 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080827205300/http://greens.org.nz/ge |archive-date=27 August 2008 }}</ref> The party strongly supports efforts to address [[Climate change in New Zealand|climate change]] based on scientific evidence, by transitioning away from the burning of fossil fuels to renewable energy production,<ref>{{cite web |title=Climate Change Policy |url=https://d3n8a8pro7vhmx.cloudfront.net/beachheroes/pages/9627/attachments/original/1594244225/Policy-Greens_Climate_Change.pdf?1594244225 |publisher=Green Party of Aotearoa New Zealand |date=8 July 2020 |access-date=18 March 2021}}</ref> as well as making [[carbon pricing]] more transparent and bringing the agricultural sector into the [[New Zealand Emissions Trading Scheme|Emissions Trading Scheme]].<ref>{{cite press release|title=Greenpeace Celebrates Green Party Commitment To End PKE |url=https://www.scoop.co.nz/stories/PO2009/S00140/greenpeace-celebrates-green-party-commitment-to-end-pke.htm |publisher=Greenpeace New Zealand |date=12 September 2020 |access-date=18 March 2021 |via=[[scoop.co.nz]]}}</ref>

==== Foreign policy ====
There have been four spokespeople Keith Locke, Kennedy Graham, Golriz Ghaharaman and currently Teanau Tuiono. Historically sympathetic in principle to national liberation, self-determination movements. This was used to justify allowing Ukrainian president to address parliament in 2022, breaking with protocol which Greens had previously objected to, with leader Marama Davidson saying she would like other oppressed nations to speak but never raised this formally.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Aotearoa |first=RNZ {{!}} Te Reo Irirangi o |date=2022-11-23 |title=Greens demand consistency over Ukraine President Zelensky invite to address Parliament |url=https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/politics/479297/greens-demand-consistency-over-ukraine-president-zelensky-invite-to-address-parliament |access-date=2026-10-14 |website=RNZ |language=en-nz}}</ref> Historically a critic of the size and role of military, although unclear whether they want civilian functions like search and rescue to be carried out by military or non-military.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Aotearoa |first=RNZ {{!}} Te Reo Irirangi o |date=2023-02-07 |title=The air force's new flying machines |url=https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/politics/552719/the-air-force-s-new-flying-machines |access-date=2026-10-15 |website=RNZ |language=en-nz}}</ref> Greens supported the Defence Capability Upgrade plan in 2019.<ref>"Question No. 8—Defence - GOLRIZ GHAHRAMAN (Green) to the Minister of Defence: What actions is the New Zealand Defence Force taking to reflect its shift in focus to addressing climate change? - 

Hon RON MARK (Minister of Defence): ... Yesterday, the Minister for Climate Change, the Hon James Shaw, and I announced the release of Responding to the Climate Crisis: An Implementation Plan, by Defence.... "

https://hansard.parliament.nz/hansard-transcript/2019-12-10/visitors-parliament-of-australia-joint-committee-o?sId=11a65336527b4096b60a59edc919ca42</ref>

Greens only persistent critics in parliament of deployment of special forces to Afghanistan which began in 2001, as well as Iraq training missions following invasion of Iraq in 2003 however during period of government in 2017 - 2020 Greens offered minimal or no opposition to deployments, an extension of all deployments for six months (late 2017) was not commented on, their extension a year later (2018) limited to a press release on the day of their announcement and asking about their future extension in parliament.<ref>Is it his intention to continue the deployments to Afghanistan and Iraq beyond 2019? James Shaw to Defence Minister

https://www.parliament.nz/en/pb/hansard-debates/rhr/document/HansS_20180918_051450000/4-question-no-4-defence</ref> Greens claimed that the withdrawl of Iraq training mission was a success of theirs but Winston Peters denied they had anything to do with the decision.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Walls |first=Jason |title=Peters plays down claims Iraq troop decision was a 'Greens Win' |url=https://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/winston-peters-a-bit-hard-to-argue-decision-to-bring-kiwi-troops-home-was-a-green-win/WHWKCWTU2CI5CJIN3QWPCIEPZY/ |access-date=2026-10-14 |website=NZ Herald |language=en-NZ}}</ref> In 2026 a former NZSAS soldier Josh Jacbson standing on the Green Party list was featured prominently in the media.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Fisher |first=David |title=From the battlefield to the ballot: NZSAS veteran stands for Parliament |url=https://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/from-the-battlefield-to-the-ballot-nzsas-veteran-josh-jacobsen-stands-for-green-party/premium/RBBPNI3GTBAMXDCXHROWSE4PRI/ |access-date=2026-10-15 |website=NZ Herald |language=en-NZ}}</ref><ref>{{Cite AV media |url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=YwCVyBBIcjU |title=The former NZSAS combat soldier standing for parliament |date=2026-08-22 |last=Q+A with Jack Tame |access-date=2026-10-15 |via=YouTube}}</ref> Jacobson served in Afghanistan and has not revealed any details such as whether he served in [[Operation Burnham]], stating only "We were there doing work that mattered."<ref>{{Cite web |last=Stead |first=Smith K. |date=2026-10-15 |title=Why are the Greens running a potential war criminal? |url=https://www.exitfromaffco.com/p/why-are-the-greens-running-a-potential-war-criminal |access-date=2026-10-17 |website=www.exitfromaffco.com |language=en}}</ref>

The Green Party has spoken out in support of [[Human rights in New Zealand|human rights]]<ref>{{cite web |url=http://greens.org.nz/campaigns/humanrights/ |title=NZ Greens: Campaigns: Human Rights |publisher=Green Party of Aotearoa New Zealand |access-date=29 June 2008 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070629201201/http://www.greens.org.nz/campaigns/humanrights/ |archive-date=29 June 2007 }}</ref> and against military operations conducted by the United States and other countries in [[Afghanistan]] and [[Iraq]].<ref>{{cite web |url=http://greens.org.nz/campaigns/peace/ |title=NZ Greens: Campaigns: JustPeace |publisher=Green Party of Aotearoa New Zealand |access-date=29 June 2008 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080704071431/http://www.greens.org.nz/campaigns/peace/ |archive-date=4 July 2008 }}</ref> The party has also expressed sympathy for the [[Palestinian]]s and criticised the [[Israeli occupation of the Palestinian Territories]].<ref>{{cite web |last1=Ghahraman |first1=Golriz |title=Green Party condemn violent displacement of Palestinians |url=https://www.greens.org.nz/green_party_condemn_violent_displacement_of_palestinians |publisher=Green Party of Aotearoa New Zealand |access-date=26 January 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231003081323/https://www.greens.org.nz/green_party_condemn_violent_displacement_of_palestinians |archive-date=3 October 2023 |date=13 May 2021 |url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |last1=Ghahraman |first1=Golriz |title=Green Party statement on the violence in Israel and Gaza |url=https://www.greens.org.nz/green_party_statement_on_the_violence_in_israel_and_gaza |publisher=Green Party of Aotearoa New Zealand |access-date=26 January 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240118100916/https://www.greens.org.nz/green_party_statement_on_the_violence_in_israel_and_gaza |archive-date=18 January 2024 |date=17 October 2023 |url-status=live}}</ref>

==== Social issues ====
The party is also known for its advocacy on numerous social issues, such as the [[Same-sex marriage in New Zealand|legalisation of marriage equality]],<ref>{{cite web |title=Green Party supports Marriage Equality |url=https://www.scoop.co.nz/stories/PA1207/S00360/green-party-supports-marriage-equality.htm  |publisher=Green Party of Aotearoa New Zealand |via=scoop.co.nz |access-date=18 March 2021}}</ref> the right to seek asylum and increasing the [[Refugees in New Zealand|refugee quota]],<ref>{{cite web |last1=Shaw |first1=James |title=Greens would double refugee quota as priority |url=https://www.greens.org.nz/greens-would-double-refugee-quota-priority |publisher=Green Party of Aotearoa New Zealand |access-date=18 March 2021 |language=en |date=30 January 2017}}</ref> and [[Gender equality in New Zealand|gender equality]].<ref>{{cite news |title=Equality for women |url=https://www.greens.org.nz/equality_for_women |newspaper=Green Party of Aotearoa New Zealand |access-date=18 March 2021 |language=en |date=2020}}</ref>

==== Indigenous rights ====
The party accepts [[Treaty of Waitangi|Te Tiriti o Waitangi]] (the [[Māori language]] version of the treaty) as the founding document of New Zealand and recognises [[Māori people|Māori]] as {{lang|mi|[[tangata whenua]]}}.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.greens.org.nz/charter|title=The Green Charter|publisher=Green Party of Aotearoa New Zealand|language=en|access-date=4 February 2017}}</ref> The party has expressed misgivings about treaty settlement process, including the government’s imposition of ‘large natural groupings’ concept on [[Hapū]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Birdling |first=Malcolm |date=November 2004 |title=HEALING THE PAST OR HARMING THE FUTURE? LARGE NATURAL GROUPINGS AND THE WAITANGI SETTLEMENT PROCESS |url=https://classic.austlii.edu.au/nz/journals/NZJlPubIntLaw/2004/15.pdf |journal=New Zealand Journal of Public and International Law |pages=259}}</ref>  For example Metiria Turei stated they "gave very serious consideration to abstaining"<ref>https://hansard.parliament.nz/hansard-transcript/2003-04-01/bills-ngati-ruanui-claims-settlement-bill?sId=2044d1a86d374acd8674dcb31eaff4bb {{Bare URL inline|date=October 2026}}</ref> on the Ngati Ruanui Claims Settlement Bill in 2003. The Greens have rejected calls to make treaty settlements full and final and see the treaty as a living document.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Burr |first=Lloyd |date=2017-10-18 |title=The 16 policies NZ First and the Greens disagree on |url=https://www.stuff.co.nz/politics/350617283/the-16-policies-nz-first-and-the-greens-disagree-on |access-date=2026-10-12 |website=Stuff |language=en}}</ref> Green Party have had an unclear position regarding the legitimacy of iwi authorities as representatives of mana whenua, and whether to oppose policies pursued by iwi authorities which contradict green values — for example at Ihumātao<ref>{{Cite web |last=Coster |first=Deena |date=2019-08-02 |title=Crown needs to do more to recognise range of Māori viewpoints - iwi leader |url=https://www.stuff.co.nz/national/114695159/crown-needs-to-do-more-to-recognise-range-of-mori-viewpoints--iwi-leader |access-date=2026-10-12 |website=Stuff |language=en}}</ref>, Shelley Bay (where Green Councillors voted with iwi authority represetantives despite opposition within the iwi authority membership to turn public land into commerical housing),<ref>{{Cite web |last=Hager |first=Nicky |date=2020-07-03 |title=The long, sorry saga of Shelly Bay |url=https://newsroom.co.nz/2020/07/03/the-long-sorry-saga-of-shelly-bay/ |access-date=2026-10-12 |website=Newsroom |language=en-US}}</ref> and the Ngati Paoa settlement (where a settlement would privatise a public reserve).<ref>{{Cite web |title=Save Point England |url=http://savepe.org.nz/ |access-date=2026-10-12 |website=savepe.org.nz |language=en}}</ref>

==== Economics ====
The Green Party economic position has shifted overtime, being once supportive of a number of unorthodox positions to becoming increasingly mainstream. Once openly skepticial of 'economic growth'<ref>https://www.oocities.org/davd.geo/jfmaiden.html Jeanette Fitzsimons maiden speech</ref>, the party has shifted to embrace 'green growth' under Russel Norman<ref>https://web.archive.org/web/20170417172635/https://www.greens.org.nz/sites/default/files/Greentimes-Winter-2012-web.pdf#1#1 {{Bare URL inline|date=October 2026}}</ref> who also described the Greens as "pro-market"<ref>{{Cite web |last=Rutherford |first=Hamish |date=27 August 2014 |title=Greens pro-market: Russel Norman |url=https://www.stuff.co.nz/national/10428953/Greens-pro-market-Russel-Norman |access-date=11 October 2026 |website=Stuff |language=en}}</ref> (including the championing of business lobby group Pure Advantage<ref>{{Cite web |title=Greens Welcome Business Leaders' Commitment To Green Economy {{!}} Scoop News |url=https://www.scoop.co.nz/stories/print.html?path=PA1211/S00250/greens-welcome-business-leaders-commitment-to-green-economy.htm#1 |access-date=12 October 2026 |website=www.scoop.co.nz}}</ref> and taking donations from some of its members <ref>{{Cite web |last=Aotearoa |first=RNZ {{!}} Te Reo Irirangi o |date=14 April 2014 |title=Labour, Greens declare donation from businessman |url=https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/politics/241654/labour,-greens-declare-donation-from-businessman |access-date=12 October 2026 |website=RNZ |language=en-nz}}</ref>). The focus on 'green growth' continued under James Shaw<ref>{{Cite web |title=NZ Climate Minister James Shaw spoke at the Beyond Growth Conference at the European Parliament on probably the only panel that was conceivably about economic growth (Focus panel 15 – Trade for… {{!}} Jennifer Wilkins |url=https://www.linkedin.com/posts/jenniferwilkinsnz_nz-climate-minister-james-shaw-spoke-at-the-activity-7064805824044421121-rbQ4 |access-date=12 October 2026 |website=LinkedIn |language=en}}</ref> who also sought to burnish the Green Party's fiscal responsibility by introducing the Budget Responsibility Rules ahead of the 2017 election.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Reddell |first=Michael |date=2017-03-26 |title=Labour/Green Budget Responsibility Rules |url=https://croakingcassandra.com/2017/03/27/labourgreen-budget-responsibility-rules/ |access-date=2026-10-12 |website=croaking cassandra |language=en}}</ref> In response to the Greens new fiscal plan announcement in 2025 some commentators have said they have made a 'dramatic break',<ref>{{Cite web |title=The Greens have broken dramatically with the James Shaw era |url=https://thespinoff.co.nz/politics/19-06-2025/the-greens-have-broken-dramatically-with-the-james-shaw-era |access-date=2026-10-15 |website=The Spinoff |language=en}}</ref> others have suggested move towards a 'economic populist' framework in their 2026 election campaign.<ref>{{Cite AV media |url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=dwrCvhGH3zM |title=Can the Greens overtake Labour? {{!}} In Brief |date=2026-09-30 |last=Public Interest NZ |access-date=2026-10-15 |via=YouTube}}</ref>

In its [[Economy of New Zealand|economic policies]], the Green Party stresses factors such as [[sustainability]], [[tax]]ing the indirect costs of pollution, and [[fair trade]]. It also states that measuring economic success should concentrate on [[measuring well-being]] rather than analysing [[economic indicators]].<ref>{{cite web |url=http://greens.org.nz/searchdocs/PR3136.html |title=Greens Call For Dinosaur GDP To Go |publisher=Green Party of Aotearoa New Zealand |date=27 March 2000 |access-date=29 June 2008 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20061015141001/http://greens.org.nz/searchdocs/PR3136.html |archive-date=15 October 2006 }}</ref> The party wants the eventual introduction of a [[universal basic income]].<ref>{{cite web |title=Income Support Policy |url=https://www.greens.org.nz/income_support_policy |publisher=Green Party of Aotearoa New Zealand |access-date=7 August 2020 |language=en}}</ref>

==== Genetically modified organisms ====
While the moratorium on genetic modification has now expired, the Greens remain heavily involved in attempts to prevent any GM releases under the new regulatory framework, and genetic engineering remains a major topic for the party.<ref>{{Cite web|last=Manhire|first=Toby|date=29 October 2019|title=Young scientists call on Greens to rethink GM stance in the cause of the climate|url=https://thespinoff.co.nz/politics/29-10-2019/young-scientists-call-on-greens-to-rethink-gm-stance-in-the-cause-of-the-climate/|access-date=1 November 2020|website=[[The Spinoff]] }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|date=28 October 2019|title=Time to break the stigma on genetic modification, for the sake of the climate|url=https://www.stuff.co.nz/environment/climate-news/116912619/time-to-break-the-stigma-on-genetic-modification-for-the-sake-of-the-climate|access-date=1 November 2020|website=[[Stuff (website)|Stuff]] |language=en}}</ref>

==== Drug law refom ====
Drug law reform was previously a major focus of the media when discussing the Greens, particular when Rastafarian Green MP Nandor Tanzcos who was the spokesperson. Undue attention lead him to drop the portfolio.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2008-06-26 |title=The legacy of Nandor |url=https://www.stuff.co.nz/national/politics/505833/The-legacy-of-Nandor |access-date=2026-10-12 |website=Stuff |language=en}}</ref> At that time Green policy was decriminalise use but has shifted to advocating for legalisation under Julie Anne Genter.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.stuff.co.nz/national/politics/87388713/legal-cannabis-in-nz-green-party-offers-green-light-to-pot-smokers|title=Legal cannabis in NZ? Green Party offers green light to pot smokers|website=[[Stuff (website)|Stuff]] |date=8 December 2016|publisher=[[Stuff NZ]]|access-date=1 September 2017|quote=Under [the party's] proposal, people would be able to legally grow and possess marijuana for personal use.}}</ref> In the 2017–2020 term of the Sixth Labour Government, medicinal cannabis was legalised,<ref name="NZ Parliament">{{cite web|title=Misuse of Drugs (Medicinal Cannabis) Amendment Bill|url=https://www.parliament.nz/en/pb/bills-and-laws/bills-proposed-laws/document/BILL_75877/misuse-of-drugs-medicinal-cannabis-amendment-bill|access-date=30 December 2018|publisher=[[New Zealand Parliament]]}}</ref> but legalisation of recreational cannabis use was [[2020 New Zealand cannabis referendum|rejected in a 2020 referendum]].<ref name="Preliminary results">{{cite news|date=30 October 2020|title=Referendum preliminary results: Yes to euthanasia reform, no to cannabis|work=[[Radio NZ]] |url=https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/national/429495/referendum-preliminary-results-yes-to-euthanasia-reform-no-to-cannabis|access-date=30 October 2020}}</ref>

==== Academic views ====
The party's ideology combines [[environmentalism]] with [[Social democracy|social democratic]] economic policies,<ref name="Miller" /> including well-funded and locally controlled public services within the confines of a [[steady-state economy]].<ref>{{cite web|title=A Sustainable Economy for New Zealand|url=https://home.greens.org.nz/sites/default/files/A_Sustainable_Economy_for_New_Zealand.pdf|publisher=Green Party of Aotearoa New Zealand|access-date=1 November 2017|date=12 November 2010}}</ref> The Green Party was founded to counter what it sees as threats to the natural environment. [[Environmental issues in New Zealand|Environmental issues]] remain its main focus 

== Organisation and structure ==
The party adopted a new constitution in 2022, named Te Waka Framework.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Palmer |first1=Russell |title=Green Party leaders 'proud' of constitution changes |url= https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/466386/green-party-leaders-proud-of-constitution-changes |access-date=10 November 2023 |work=[[Radio New Zealand]] |date=3 May 2022}}</ref> This is a Te Tiriti-based structure that is derived from the party's charter and commitment to [[Treaty of Waitangi|Te Tiriti o Waitangi]]. The framework contains four sections: Te Waka, Ngā Haumi, Te Hāpai, and Ngā Tumu, and is based on the journey of a [[Waka (canoe)|waka]].<ref>{{cite web |title=Constitution of the Green Party of Aotearoa New Zealand |url=https://elections.nz/assets/party-files/Constitution-of-the-Green-Party-of-Aotearoa-New-Zealand-June-2022.pdf |publisher=Green Party of Aotearoa New Zealand |access-date=10 November 2023}}</ref>

{| class="wikitable"
!Te Waka
|Te Waka covers the governance and policy development and includes areas such as Kaunihera (Council), Te Rōpū Pounamu, Policy Hub, and Kaumātua Kākāriki.
|-
!Ngā Haumi
|Ngā Haumi are the administration and operation aspects of the party and covers the party office.
|-
!Te Hāpai
|Te Hāpai covers membership engagement and representation. It is instructed by and answerable to the membership and includes provinces, branches, and networks. One of the decision making bodies of the party, Member Assembly, also falls under Te Hāpai, as well as Te Awa, the party's magazine.
|-
!Ngā Tumu
|Ngā Tumu are the leaders of the party and include both parliamentary caucus and local government caucus.
|}

=== Provinces and branches ===
A province is a collection of branches which has sufficient sense of common identity defined by natural geographical boundaries.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web|date=2016|title=Constitution of the Green Party of Aotearoa New Zealand|url=https://members.greens.org.nz/sites/default/files/2019-11/Green%20Party%20Constitution%2C%20last%20revd%20August%202019.pdf|website=elections.org.nz}}</ref> Branches are a collection of members with an [[New Zealand electorates|electorate]]-based geographical area of responsibility.<ref name=":0" />

=== Networks ===
There are a number of identity or interest-based networks across the party.<ref>{{Cite web|title=For people and planet|url=https://www.greens.org.nz/contact|access-date=1 August 2020|website=Green Party of Aotearoa New Zealand|language=en}}</ref> These include:
*[[Degrowth]] Greens<ref>{{Cite web |title=For people and planet |url=https://www.greens.org.nz/degrowth_greens |access-date=12 November 2024 |website=Green Party of Aotearoa New Zealand |language=en}}</ref>
*Green Women (a [[Women's wing|network for women members]])
*Inclusive Greens (a network for members living with a disability)
*Pasifika Greens (a network for members with [[Pasifika New Zealanders|Pasifika]] ancestry)
*Rainbow Greens (a [[LGBTQ wing|network for LGBTQIA+ members]])
*Rural Greens (a network for members with interests in rural and agricultural issues)
*GreenLeft (a network for left-wing, [[anti-capitalist]] members)<ref name="Spinoff">{{cite web |url= https://thespinoff.co.nz/politics/04-10-2018/socialism-is-back-baby-and-it-doesnt-want-your-vote/ |title= Socialism is back, baby, and it doesn't want your vote |last= Braae |first= Alex |date= 4 October 2018 |website=[[The Spinoff]] |access-date= 12 December 2020}}</ref>
*Te Roopu Pounamu (a Māori network)<ref name=":0" />
*Union Greens (representing trade unions)
*[[Young Greens (New Zealand)|Young Greens]]

== Local government ==

=== Campaigns ===

====2013====
In the [[2013 New Zealand local elections|2013 local elections]], the Greens won three city council and two regional council seats in [[Wellington]],<ref>{{cite web|title=2013 election results|url=http://www.gw.govt.nz/2013results/|publisher=[[Greater Wellington Regional Council]]|access-date=24 September 2017}}</ref> a council seat in [[Dunedin]],<ref>{{cite web|title=2013 Dunedin City Council Final Results|url=http://www.dunedin.govt.nz/your-council/electoral-information/2013-election-results/dcc-results|publisher=[[Dunedin City Council]]|access-date=24 September 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150923221236/http://www.dunedin.govt.nz/your-council/electoral-information/2013-election-results/dcc-results|archive-date=23 September 2015|url-status=dead}}</ref> and also enjoyed success in [[Christchurch]] and [[Gisborne, New Zealand|Gisborne]].{{citation needed|date=June 2022}}

====2016====
During the [[2016 New Zealand local elections|2016 local elections]], Green Dunedin candidate Aaron Hawkins was re-elected to the [[Dunedin City Council]] and was joined by the Green Party's first successful local or parliamentary  [[Pasifika New Zealander|Pasifika]] candidate, Councillor [[Marie Laufiso]].<ref>{{cite web|title=Dunedin City Council Final Results – 2016 Triennial Elections|url=http://www.dunedin.govt.nz/your-council/electoral-information/2016-election-results/dcc-results|publisher=[[Dunedin City Council]]|access-date=4 November 2017}}</ref> During the [[2016 Wellington local elections|2016 Wellington local election]], four Green candidates [[Sue Kedgley]], Iona Pannett, Sarah Free, and David Lee were elected onto the [[Greater Wellington Regional Council]] and the Lambton, Eastern, and Southern Wards of the [[Wellington City Council]].<ref>{{cite web|title=2016 Triennial Elections|url=http://www.gw.govt.nz/assets/Elections-2016/Wellington-Constituency-Preliminary-Result.pdf|publisher=[[Greater Wellington Regional Council]]|access-date=4 November 2017}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|title=Wellington City Council 2016 Triennial Elections|url=https://wellington.govt.nz/~/media/your-council/elections/2016/files/final-results.pdf|publisher=[[Wellington City Council]]|access-date=4 November 2017}}</ref> Several Green candidates also contested seats on the [[Auckland Council]], local boards, and licensing trusts during the [[2016 Auckland local elections|2016 Auckland local body elections]].<ref>{{cite web|title=Ward Councillors|url=https://www.aucklandcouncil.govt.nz/about-auckland-council/elections/elections-2016/Documents/ward-councillors.pdf|publisher=[[Auckland Council]]|access-date=4 November 2017|archive-date=7 November 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171107004318/https://www.aucklandcouncil.govt.nz/about-auckland-council/elections/elections-2016/Documents/ward-councillors.pdf|url-status=dead}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|title=Local board members|url=https://www.aucklandcouncil.govt.nz/about-auckland-council/elections/elections-2016/Documents/local-board-members.pdf|publisher=[[Auckland Council]]|access-date=4 November 2017|archive-date=3 February 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180203152548/https://www.aucklandcouncil.govt.nz/about-auckland-council/elections/elections-2016/Documents/local-board-members.pdf|url-status=dead}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|title=Licensing trusts|url=https://www.aucklandcouncil.govt.nz/about-auckland-council/elections/elections-2016/Documents/licensing-trusts.pdf|publisher=[[Auckland Council]]|access-date=4 November 2017}}</ref>

In addition, Brent Barrett was elected to [[Palmerston North City Council]].<ref name="Manawatu Standard 9 Jan 2022">{{cite news |last1=Rankin |first1=Janine |title=Labour and the Greens look for more local body candidates |url=https://www.stuff.co.nz/manawatu-standard/news/127457597/labour-and-the-greens-look-for-more-local-body-candidates |access-date=13 November 2022 |work=[[Manawatu Standard]] |publisher=[[Stuff (company)|Stuff]] |date=9 January 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221020111041/https://www.stuff.co.nz/manawatu-standard/news/127457597/labour-and-the-greens-look-for-more-local-body-candidates |archive-date=20 October 2022}}</ref>

====2019====
The [[2019 New Zealand local elections]] were the most successful local body elections ever for the party, culminating in 42 successful candidates.<ref>{{Cite web|title=About|url=https://www.greens.org.nz/about|access-date=30 September 2020|website=Green Party of Aotearoa New Zealand|language=en|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200326183529/https://www.greens.org.nz/about|archive-date=26 March 2020}}</ref> Notably, [[Aaron Hawkins (politician)|Aaron Hawkins]] was elected [[Mayor of Dunedin]], becoming the first Green Party candidate to ever win a mayoralty in New Zealand.<ref>{{Cite news |url= https://www.stuff.co.nz/national/116921443/dunedin-welcomes-aaron-hawkins--the-countrys-first-green-party-mayor| title=Dunedin welcomes Aaron Hawkins – the country's first Green Party mayor |work=[[Stuff (website)|Stuff]] |access-date=12 February 2020}}</ref>

In addition, Brent Barrett was re-elected to the Palmerston North City Council and was joined by a second Green candidate Renee Dingwall. Future Green MP [[Teanau Tuiono]] also ran for the position of [[Mayor of Palmerston North]] but was defeated by the incumbent Grant Smith.<ref name="Manawatu Standard 9 Jan 2022" />

====2022====
During the [[2022 New Zealand local elections]], ten Green branded candidates were elected to local government positions.<ref>{{cite web |title=Our Local Government Representatives |url=https://www.greens.org.nz/our_local_government_representatives |publisher=Green Party of Aotearoa New Zealand |access-date=9 November 2022 }}</ref> Though Aaron Hawkins was defeated in his bid to be [[2022 Dunedin mayoral election|re-elected]] as Mayor of Dunedin, the Green-endorsed [[Tory Whanau]] was elected as [[Mayor of Wellington]].<ref>{{cite news |last1=McNeilly |first1=Hamish |title='A very public divorce': Aaron Hawkins on losing the Dunedin mayoralty |url=https://thespinoff.co.nz/politics/22-10-2022/a-very-public-divorce-aaron-hawkins-on-losing-the-dunedin-mayoralty |access-date=9 November 2022 |work=[[The Spinoff]] |date=22 October 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221027180226/https://thespinoff.co.nz/politics/22-10-2022/a-very-public-divorce-aaron-hawkins-on-losing-the-dunedin-mayoralty |archive-date=27 October 2022|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |title=Whanau bucks trend in referendum on leadership |url=https://www.newsroom.co.nz/whanau-bucks-trend-in-referendum-on-leadership |access-date=9 November 2022 |work=[[Newsroom (website)|Newsroom]] |date=8 October 2022 |language=en-AU |first=Marc |last=Daalder |archive-date=9 October 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221009064036/https://www.newsroom.co.nz/whanau-bucks-trend-in-referendum-on-leadership#Echobox=1665215993-1 |url-status=live }}</ref>

Green councillor [[Tamatha Paul]] was [[2022 Wellington City mayoral election|elected]] to the [[Wellington City Council]] (WCC) and became the chair of its new environment and infrastructure committee.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Gourley |first1=Erin |title=Labour, Green councillors to lead key committees on new Wellington City Council |url=https://www.stuff.co.nz/dominion-post/wellington-top-stories/130411523/labour-green-councillors-to-lead-key-committees-on-new-wellington-city-council |access-date=8 November 2022 |work=[[Stuff (website)|Stuff]] |date=8 November 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221108042724/https://www.stuff.co.nz/dominion-post/wellington-top-stories/130411523/labour-green-councillors-to-lead-key-committees-on-new-wellington-city-council |archive-date=8 November 2022|url-status=live}}</ref> In addition, Laurie Foon and Nīkau Wi Neera were elected to the WCC's Southern General Ward and Te Whanganui-a-Tara Māori ward.<ref>{{cite web |title=Wellington City Council: 2022 Triennial Elections |url=https://wellington.govt.nz/-/media/your-council/elections/2022/wellington-city-council-2022-triennial-elections---final-stv-result.pdf |publisher=[[Wellington City Council]] |access-date=17 November 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221020062552/https://wellington.govt.nz/-/media/your-council/elections/2022/wellington-city-council-2022-triennial-elections---final-stv-result.pdf |archive-date=20 October 2022 |url-status=live}}</ref>

In addition, Yadana Saw, Thomas Nash, and Quentin Duthie were elected on the Green Party ticket to the [[Wellington Region|Greater Wellington Regional Council]].<ref>{{cite web|title=2022 Election Results and Returns |url=https://www.gw.govt.nz/your-council/elections/2022-election-results-and-returns/ |access-date=17 November 2022 |publisher=[[Greater Wellington Regional Council]] |date=16 November 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221018043018/https://www.gw.govt.nz/your-council/elections/2022-election-results-and-returns/ |archive-date=18 October 2022 |url-status=live}}</ref>

Green councillor Brent Barrett was re-elected for a third term on the [[Palmerston North City Council]] (PNCC).<ref>{{cite news |last1=Lacy |first1=Judith |title=Grant Smith easily re-elected as Palmerston North mayor |url=https://www.nzherald.co.nz/manawatu-guardian/news/grant-smith-easily-re-elected-as-palmerston-north-mayor/73ZNG6OST4RQ24YHX42UFUIUEY/ |access-date=13 November 2022 |work=[[The New Zealand Herald]] |date=11 October 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221025020142/https://www.nzherald.co.nz/manawatu-guardian/news/grant-smith-easily-re-elected-as-palmerston-north-mayor/73ZNG6OST4RQ24YHX42UFUIUEY/ |archive-date=25 October 2022|url-status=live}}</ref> In addition, Kaydee Zabelin was elected to the PNCC on the Green ticket.<ref>{{cite web |title=Final results – Palmerston North City Council 2022 local elections |url=https://www.pncc.govt.nz/files/assets/public/documents/participate-palmy/elections/2022-elections/final-pncc-lge-results-2022.pdf |publisher=[[Palmerston North City Council]] |access-date=17 November 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221014112346/https://www.pncc.govt.nz/files/assets/public/documents/participate-palmy/elections/2022-elections/final-pncc-lge-results-2022.pdf |archive-date=14 October 2022 |date=14 October 2022 |url-status=live}}</ref>

In [[Otago]], [[Marie Laufiso]] was elected to the [[Dunedin City Council]] as a councillor.<ref>{{cite web |title=2022 Election results |url=https://www.dunedin.govt.nz/council/electoral-information/2022-election-results |publisher=[[Dunedin City Council]] |access-date=9 November 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221103233810/https://www.dunedin.govt.nz/council/electoral-information/2022-election-results |archive-date=3 November 2022 |date=31 October 2022 |url-status=live}}</ref> In addition, Alan Somerville was elected to the Dunedin Regional Constituency of the [[Otago Regional Council]].<ref>{{cite web |title=Media release: ORC ushers in new triennium of Councillors |url=https://www.orc.govt.nz/news-and-events/news-and-media-releases/2022/october/orc-ushers-in-new-triennium-of-councillors |publisher=[[Otago Regional Council]] |access-date=17 November 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221014112036/https://www.orc.govt.nz/news-and-events/news-and-media-releases/2022/october/orc-ushers-in-new-triennium-of-councillors |archive-date=14 October 2022 |date=14 October 2022 |url-status=live}}</ref> In July 2024, Laufiso resigned from the party over the ousting of Tana, becoming an independent city councillor.<ref>John, Mark "[https://www.odt.co.nz/news/dunedin/dcc/laufiso-resigns-green-party-over-tana-issue Laufiso resigns from Green Party over Tana issue]" ''Otago Daily Times'', 29 July 2024. Retrieved 23 March 2025.</ref>

====2024 Wellington by-election====
In February 2024, Green Party candidate Georgie Rogers was elected to the Pukehīnau/Lambton General Ward in the [[Wellington City Council]]. The ward had been vacated by [[Tamatha Paul]], who had been elected to Parliament as a Green MP during the 2023 New Zealand general election.<ref>{{cite news |title=Green Party candidate Geordie Rogers wins Wellington City Council by-election |url=https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/509775/green-party-candidate-geordie-rogers-wins-wellington-city-council-by-election |access-date=23 February 2024 |work=[[Radio New Zealand]] |date=21 February 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240221190944/https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/509775/green-party-candidate-geordie-rogers-wins-wellington-city-council-by-election |archive-date=21 February 2024|url-status=live}}</ref>

==Leadership==
The party has six equal status office holders that form their leadership group:

* two co-leaders (one female and one of any gender, one of whom must be Māori)
* two party co-convenors (one female and one of any gender)
* two policy co-convenors (one female and one of any gender)

The co-leaders lead the caucus, the party co-convenors lead the party executive, and the policy co-convenors lead the policy committee. The leadership group facilitates high level discussion and co-ordination between the three committees.

===Co-leaders===
{{anchor|Male co-leaders|Female co-leaders}}
{{Main|Co-leaders of the Green Party of Aotearoa New Zealand}}Historically, the Green Party had one male and one female as co-leaders, but in May 2022 members voted to require one leader be female and one be [[Māori people|Māori]].<ref>{{cite news |first=Russell |last=Palmer | url= https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/466386/green-party-leaders-proud-of-constitution-changes | title=Green Party leaders 'proud' of constitution changes | work=[[Radio New Zealand]] | date=3 May 2022 |access-date=11 May 2022}}</ref> [[Marama Davidson]] has been the female co-leader since 2018. [[Chlöe Swarbrick]] became co-leader in March 2024, succeeding [[James Shaw (New Zealand politician)|James Shaw]], who had been elected as male co-leader in 2015.

===Co-convenors===

===Policy co-convenors===
Policy co-convenors are the leaders of the policy committee, which is autonomous from both the caucus and the party executive. While lower in public profile than the party co-convenors, the policy co-convenors are considered to have the same status as the party co-convenors, and are elected in the same way. As of May 2022, the party's new constitution requires one female policy co-convenor and one policy co-convenor of any gender.
